DAITWILS, Airily fairily, floating and fluttering Daffodils, welcomest flowers of the year'! Ire come when the hoarse winds of March are stM mut-

- . tenng Bleak o'er the snow-fleckered landscape droar. Deep, deep in winter-sleep. Nature all wearily Lay for long months, and so chill was hefloreath That the cold of it crept to our heavy hearts drearily, Hashing them, crushing them, nigh unto death I swing out your goldenkells, beautiful daffodils! Swing them and ring them among your green spires Ring in the spring-time! ring in the life that thrills! Wake to their love-songs the wild woodland choirs! lie that hath ears to en, pausing and listening, Hears in his heart of hearts your mystic chine; Deep in his soul it thrills, while, with eyes glistening, Unto your music his heart beats time! Swing out your golden bells, sweet dainty daffodils! Swing them and ring them, and ring tim, again, Now is spring-tide with us— Come to Abide with us Lightening and brightening o'er ;alley and plain! O'er the cloud-shadowed hills, radiant daffodils! Chase the dark gloom that chills, till it departs, Pealing your mystic chime, Ring in the glad spring-time, Life to all Nature 4 and joy to our hearts! • —Good Words. R. tlfacaultry&ovenson.
'TICE CLIFTON MAID. A LEGEND OF CLIFTON, NEAR NOTTINGILLIt.

Bail! goddess fair, whose favour dost inspire The humblest mortal with poetic fire; Thou who aloneof deities c,anst impart To man—to lowly man—the poet's art; Thou who, when earth was young in long-pastleays, Taught Israel's Shepherd-King to sing his lays; Thou, mighty goddess ! grant me my desire, And with thy magic touch attune my lyre. _ - Where hasteithe silver Trent to meet the sea, Past meadows green and woodland scenery, Stands Clifton fair, whither at break of day The youthful poet* loved to wend his way; And nigh the village, clothed in summer's green Or winter's bareness, Clifton Grove is seen. Two centuries ago' the Clifton Maid, Margaret her name, dwelt in this "hamlet's shad•-;z" Fair as the hour when Night's dark shadows flee, Beloved by all the:rustic swains was she; Yet in the maiden's heart but on alone: Found a responsive feeling to his Own, And he was Bateman. Often when the sun Had left his regal court and day was done, When the shy moon showed once again her face, And twinkling stars came from their hiding-place, The happy couple Wandered 'neath the trees, Whose leaves soft-rustled in the gentle breeze, And murmured vows of faithfulness and love, Which angels heard and registered above. But soon misfortune's clouds obscured the day, Harsh Fate placed.troubles in peer Bateman's way, And he for three long years was forced to part From Jur, the idol of his breaking heart; And on a distant Shore—to him how drear!— Dwell, far away from all that' beheld dear. Sad was the parting. (Gloomy was the night ; The Storm-king howled; the stars in their affright Trembled and shuddered, and the moon withdrew • Behind Night's dusky curtains, fearing too; The rain descended, and while lightning glared _ _
•:;os

and while lightning The roar of thunder o'er the storm was heard! Then broke the maid her golden ring in two—' Half kept herself, half gave her lover true. " Keep this," she cried, "and when, thy exile o'er. 77. Thou seekest once again Britannia's shore, By the just God, Who-rules the land and sea, 1 If Margaret thou shalt-find untrue to thee, , May the fottl fiends-Of 'hell and night combine To take away this wretched life of mine, . And cast me o'er yen cliffs to find a tomb In Clifton Deeps! Suet, Bateman be my doom?' IA

Three years had passed,and Bateman stood onnealiKete Upon his own, his wellerced native shore. Gaily he hastened on to claim his bride, But soon his cup of joy was:clashed aside; . For, in his absence, lo I another came And sought the maid; helad a noble name: iSf."";' And wealth to buy the luxuries of life, And, Margaret yielding, soon became his wife. .. Maddened with grief, poor-Bateman rushed away, ;77 And sought the ,ffrove where in a happier day- He oft had strolled with Margaret at his side— The Margaret who was now another's bride. He neared the Trent, whose waters murmuring loud Recalled to Bateman's naind.what Bhe had vowed Upon that parting night. Filled with despair. The frenzied lover rushed to drown his care. Bounding, he cleared the haughty cliff's proud breast, And 'nelth the waters of the Trent found rest.' And what of Margaret? When six months had fled, Behold, she lay upon a dying bed; And, says the legend, those who watched around Fell fast asleep, and on awakening found . The dying one had fled! And there are those Who say that in the night a cry arose, • Piercing and shrill; and further 'tis averred , A sound as of a heavy fall was heard. The stranger still is shown the grass-grown way By which the demons bore the wife away To find in Clifton Deeps a watery tomb, And thus fulfil her sMf-predestined doom. Preston, Feb.. 1885. EXCELSIOR. *Henry Kirke White is the poet bare referred to.

A smart old lady, being called into court as a witness, grew impatient at the questions put to ker, and told the judge that she would stand down, for he was " raly,one of the most inquisitive old gentlemen she ever seen. ' irn Irishman, who lives with a vegetarian, writes to a friend that if he wants to know what illigant living is he must come to his house, where the breakfast consists of nothing, and the supper of what was left at breakfast. A lover received the following note on Valentine's day, accompanied by a beautiful bouquet Deer —, I send bi the boy a buckett of flours. There is like my love for u. The nibs shaid menes kepe dark. The dog fenil menes lam ure slaive. Roses red and possis pail; my luv for u shall never Isle." One day a pompous bailie of a rising Scottish town overtook upon the road Cuddle Nellie, a well known character in the district. "Get out or the way," said the baillie ; "don't you see my horse is frightened at your ass?" " shure it shouldna be," replied Nellie, "seem' it's carryin' ane every day." Just as a country lover dropped on his knees and be- gan popping the question, a poodle, who thought the proceedings rather strange, made a rush at him. With remarkable nerve for a woman, the girl reached over, grabbed the dog by the neck, at the same time calmly exclaiming, "Go on, George, dear. I'm listening to what you are saying." Admiral Make, when a captain, waS sent with a small squadron to the West Indies on a secret expedition against the Spanish settlement. It happened in an en- gagement that one of the ships blew up, which damped the spirits of the crew; but Blake, who was not to be subdued by One unsuccessful occurrence, called out to his men, "Well, my lads, you have seen an English ship blown up; let's see what a figure a [Spanish one-,will, make in the same situation?' This well-timed harangue raised their spirits immediately, and in less than an hour he set his antagonist on fire. "There, my lads," said he, "I knew we should have our revenge soon." When mesical pitchforks were first introduced, a cer- tain precentor thought he might be the better of one, and ordered an Edinburgh carrier to bring it. The honest carrier, who had never heard of any other pitch- fork but that used in the barnyard, purchased one at least 10ft. long. It was late on Saturday evening before he came home, and, as a message had been left to bring it up when he came to church next day, he marched into the churchyard before the bell rang, where the master of song was standing among a group of vil- lagers. "Aweel, John, here's the pitchfork you wanted, but I can tell you I ne'er thought muckle o' your singin' before, and I'm sair mistaken gin you'll sing ony better now." READING AND WRMNG IN THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY. "The art of reading," says Lord Eames, "made very slaw Progress to encourage printing in England; capital punishment for murder was remitted if the crimmal could but read." In a letter, dated 1518, there is an account of a seditious paper which Twas stuck on St. Paul's Church, and, in order to discover who had writ- ten it, the Aldermen of London and the Prity Council- lors were ordered to go round all the warder to see all write who could." The issuing of suclian order as this , shows to what a limited extent writingynust have been known. It would appear country gentlemen were not better scribes than the citizens, for in a book :printed about this time it is gravely suggested that those gentle- en who could not write might note anything down by "cutting knotches in a stick.". ANIMALS AND Muste.--(Jurious effects have been pro- duced on animals by music. A dog is mentioned by Fetis which had such a dislike to the sound of a violin that he began to howl in anticipation as soon as he saw it touched. The same author gives an account of a lizard which would come out of an old wall, where he had established a domicile, on hearing the adagio to Mozart's Quartet in C, but would not pay the same compliment to any other piece. The pigeon that would fly from his dove-house and perch on the parlour window to hear liandel's air of "Spera Si, mio caro," is well known. Lenz, in his anecdotes of animals, relates one of an elephant, who paid no attention to the performance of an orchestra in his vicinity until they played ",Char- mante Grabriele," when he appeared much pleased, keep- tag time with his trunk, and was particularly attracted by the musician who played the horn .—Girl's Own Paper. Nothing but the Infinite pity is sufficient for the in- finite pathos of human life.—John Inglesant. "Well," said an Irish attorney, "if it plaze the court if I'm wrong in this, I have another point that is equally conclusive.' It is a happy thing for us that this is reall*ll we have to concern ourselves about—what to do next. No man can do the second thing. He can do the first.—Geo.,l Macdonald. "I am surprised, John r said an old lady when she! found the butler helping himself to some of the 'finest old port. "So am I, ma'am; I thought you had gone* out !' was the reply: With patient mind thy course of duty run; .God nothing does, nor suffers to be done, But thou wouldst do thyself, couldst thou buteee The end of all events as well as He.—Byrsest. Not long since the late Jere. Black, the Americein jurist, in examining a witness who had been in the army, said, "Come, soldier, tell us what you know of this matter." "I am no soldier, I am an officer," haughtily 'responded the witness; whereupon the old lawyer calmly said, "Well, then, officer, who is no soldier, tell les what you know." The vain fellow was crushed. Josh Billings was asked, "How fast does soundttravel?" Ills idea is that it depends a good deal upon'the noise you are talking about. "The sound of a dinner horn, for instance, travels half a mile in a second; 'oithile an invitation tew get up in the morning I have known to be 3 quarters uv an hour goin' 2 pair of stairssand*then not hes( strength enuff left to be heard." Charity of speech is as divine a thing as charity of action. The tongue that spea,keth no evil isots lovely as the hand which giveth alms. To judge no one harshly, to misconceive no man's motives, to believe things 'are what they seem to be until they are proved otherwise, to temper judgment with mercy, surely is quite as good as to build up churches, establish asylums,-andto found colleges. The poet Waller dedicated a splendid proi3xicticay to Oliver Cromwell, hailing his accession to power a glorious event. Presently Charles the Second -came' to the throne of his ancestors, and Wailer produced another panegyric for the honour and glory of the'king. The witty monarch read it, and, turning to Waller, observed, "The poem you wrote on Cromwell was superior." -The reply was unequalled. "I own it, your Majesty,'L said Waller," poets write better on fiction than onitnith." Edwin Arnold's latest poem You ask me, dear, what perfect thing I find la all nty wandering These ancient Sanskrit scrolls amid, Where ludia's deepest heart is hid., Nothing, I answer, half so wise As one glance from your gentle eyes.; Nothing so tender or so true As one word interchanged with you. Madame de Steel was a pitiless talker. -Some:gentle- men who wished to teach her a lesson introduced a per. to her, who, they said, was a very learned man. The blue-stocking received him graciously, but, eagerteopro- duce an impression, began to talk away, and ,ablaid 'a thousand questions, as engrossed with herself that she did not notice that hervisiter made no reply. 'Whenthe visit was over the gentleman asked 'Corinne how -she liked her friend. "A most delightftil man 1" was :the reply; "what wit and learning r' lierethelaugh-same in—the visitor was deaf and dumb. PRESCRIPTIONS FOR PITS.—For a fit ot extravagance: Go to the workhouse, er speak to timiinmates of sogaol, and you will be convinced. For a fit of ambition sGo to the churchyard and read the granestones. Therwill tell you the end of man in his best estate. For a- fit- of ; passion:. Walk out in the open air. You may-speak your r mind to the winds without hurting annone; or prochini- ing yourself to be a simpleton. Fdi a :fitof idleness': Count the ticking of a clock. Do this 'f or one hour,sisid you will be glad to pall off your cost and-work .man. For a fit of reining: Look about 'fee 'the ha - nd the blind,And visit the bedridden, thesifflicted,,a4 the deranged, and they will make you ashamed of cam- Salaining of your light afflictions. For a fit,offenvy : GO, and see how many who keep their carriages are afflicted With rheumatism, gout, and dropsy, how many walk abroad on crutches, or stay-at home wrappetrita flannel, and how many are subject-to epilepsy and apoplexy. ST INTERESTING PROEIDEM SOLTED.—The loequen attempts of railway trains to pass each tither ~,on thl saves track have been attended so uniformily with dims= troika consequences that it has come to be the general belie that theleat is impossible, and that engineers will 'do well to desist from further efforts to accomplish hi: To, the ordinary mind it seems inevitable that;ff Awci trains approach each other on the same track, and do not -i.cken their speed, a collision must mane. ;Tint thereis a man in Connecticut Whose mind is notardinary:. Of ccurze, we do not mean by "such a statemerat :to sinuaterthat the Nutmeg State possesses only wee man gifted -with extraordinary mental endowments. The , woods there are full of them, but, SO far as heard from. e there is ouly one who has exercised his genius in sailvingl the problesn of how to enable two 'trains to pass QM -the, ! _same track without collision. The -plan of this ingenious( person is very simple, as all really great plans and ideas, He pni.iposes to place on the front of every locoaao-i doe going itahne direction a long inclined plane, upon', . which are tom rails. These come dose to the track at, , the forward ead of the plane, and at The hinder end anal connected with other rails that run along the tops of the - cars, and downito the main track again .on another in- dined plane in-the rear. When the tratic:provided with this Attachment meets another on the same track, theilatter simply-goes over the former, its weight making the connection ofeihe front of the inclined :plane and the rails ofthe main track perfect, and acting ateite same time as a brake on the speed of the train underaegth. If this inventioa ha& beenonde a few years sooner,the number of double-track•roads in the country would net now be half so great as it-is. A single track, with occasional switches tor heavy freight trains, would answer all sour- poses, and tbe cost of .'constructing railroads would be decreased 26 per cent. The system will, of course, be adopted immediately on single-track roads, and within a few years the sensation of rioting over or under another moving train will beeo common as to pass almost un- noticed. America is a great country !—Atlantie Ocean. TILE FARMER'S HIRED stair.--" I'M kinder COakin' around the market for a hired man," he exclaimed., as he stopped at one of the stands and nibbled at an onion. "1 kinder need one, but yet 1 kinder hope I shan't be able to find him." "How's that r "Wall, there ain't no profit in a hired man no more, No, sir, he's no good any 12nger." "What's the reason ?" "Oh, a dozen reasofis. First and foremost, times have changed, and the hired man has changed with 'em, Ah ! sir, it makes me sad when I think of the hired men we had before the war—great big, fellers with Che strength of an oic and the vim of a locomotive. I didn't have to holler my lungs out to git one of 'em out of bed at three o'clock in the morning, and it was all I could do to coax 'em to go to bed at ten o'clock at night. I'm afraid that we shan't never see no more hired men wuth keepin' around for their board." "That's sad." "It's sad, and more, too. Now, as I said, I want a hired man. I'm willing to pay all or 812 a month for a smart one. Some farmers want a man to work all day and all night, but that ain't me. I have never asked one to git out of bed before three o'clock—never. I allus give my man three-quar- ters of an hour at noon, unless the hogs git out or cattle break in, or a shower is coming up. After a man has worked-right along for nine hoursjhis system wants at least half an hour to brace up in. They don't quit work on some farms till eight o'clock, but I'm no such slave- driver. At half-past seven I tell my man to knock off. All he has to do after that is to feed the stock, cut a little wood, mow some grass for the horses, milk four cows. fill up the water trough, start a smudge in the smoke-house, and pull a few weeds in the garden. I never had a hired man who didn't grow:fat on my work, and they allus left me feeling that they:hadn't half- earned their wages." He stopped long enough to wipe away a tear from his eye, ands,hen went on— 'And now look at the hired man of to-day! He wears white shirts and collars. He won't eat with a knife. He wants nap- kins when he eats, and if we don't hang up eclean towel once a week he,wipes on his handkercher.*l tall him at three and gets up at six. He wants a whole hour at noon and after supper he trots off to a singing school or sits down to a newspaper. Fifteen years ago if my, hired man was sick for half a day I could dock him If he died I could take out a month's wages for the trouble. Be was glad to get store orders for his pay, and he would wash in the rain-barrel and wipe on the clothes line. There's bin a change, sir—an awful change; and if a reaction don't set in pretty soon you will witness the downfall of agriculture in this country." "Then you won't hire another ?" "Wall, I can't just say, Work is powerfully pressing, but I'm going slow. Before I hire him I want to know whether he's a man who'll pass his plate for more meat and taters, and whether we've got to use starch in doing up his shirts. The last man I had took me to task for not holding family prayers twice a day, and after I had done so for three months I found it was only a game of his to beat me out of half an hour a, day. No, no; though I kinder need one, I kinder hope and think I Nshan't be able to find him !"—American Paper.

- - THE POPE AND THE PAPACY.—Mondty was the rope's birth,lay, and the Sacred College of Cardinais waited upon his Holiness to offer their congratulat'ons. In the course of his reply, Pope Leo expressed deep regret at the present position of Papacy, which had been giv-n up to the enemy, who was able to take away what was left to it by means of laws and guarantees, which constituted evidence of the tiooliation of the Propaganda. His LI olimzes, in conclusion, declared that neither he nor his successors could ever accept such a state of thing. VaTE OF CENSURE ON MR. FORSTER, M r.-A meetin of the Liberal Four Hundred was held at Bradford, on Mon- day, to consider Mr. Forster's attitude towards the Govern- ment on the recent vote of censure. It was carried with only One diss-ntient, "That the Bradford Liberal Four Hun- dred regrets that Mr. Forster has felt it his duty to record his vote against Mr. Gladstone's Government, and affirms its strongest conviction that in taking this course Mr. Fors- ter has acted in direct opposition to the wishes and opinions of the Liberal party in Bradford." This Is the second vote of censure passed on the right hon. gentleman by his con- stituents, the previous one being in May last. • • • • - •••

THE CRIIISE_OF_PRINCE_EDWARD

AND PRIN'CIt GEORGE. 'The 'Editor of the English Illustrated Magazine the place of honour this month to a series of extracts l'reNthe diary of Prince Edward and Prinee George of Wales, having reference to their stay in West and South Australia. The forthcoming volume from which they are taken contains an account of subsequent visits to 'Victoria, New South Wales, and Queensland; and the ,publishers have therefore taken the opportunity of sup- .plementing the text with illustrations of those places. We have seldom read a more interesting diary, written in a pleasant, hearty, unassuming spirit, and exhibiting the greatest satisfaction at the kindness with which they 'were received. Here is an account of their first day in the bush :—" We rode on to Marblup, where we arrived about 4 p.m., thirty !stiles from Albany, at Mr. Young's ,farmhouse and clearing. The mantelpieces, the tables, and all the furniture, are made of mahogany, or the darker jarrah wood. The broad, large inglenook, with seats on either side, looks uncommonly snug with the Ikon dogs for the logs, a pile of which last are stacked in the verandah outside, so as to be conveniently handy for throwing on the fire all night through. Mr. and Mrs. Young, their two sons and two daughters, gave us a hearty welcome, and, after taking a draught of -warm ' fresh milk (of which there seems an inexhaustible sup- ply all over the place), we walk up to the -small -shanty in which we are to stay. This cousista.of two rooms completely empty and with bare doors, -each, however, has a large open fireplace and plenty of jarmh wood stacked for use during the night Two grand wood fires 4are already burning, bright and dry, such a contrast to what we have had for the last few weeks on board ship. A small two-wheeled cart that has brought our mat- tresses and rugs, and what few things we wanted for the night, has arrived before us, and we ,proceed at once to make our toilet in the open air, for there is plenty of fresh water in the tank outside, .and a smaltwooden trough does duty by turns for each of the party. Bevis, a large kangaroo dog, a sort of huge, brown, Scotch greyhound, looks on as we make ourselves ready for Mrs. Young's tea-supper, for which we return ttathe farm- house, and there every one was very hearty and jolly, and did ample justice to the fowls, minced kangaroo the jam, cream, sconces, and no end of beautiful fresh milk and butter, such as we had nettasted since we had left England (for there is none, or very little, ef either of these two last at the Cape or in South America). The day has been cloudy, but there has been no rain; though every one says there is every sign of it being wet and windy to-morrow, one of which is thatthe hills •intthe distance are intensely blue. After tea found ourway up across the paddock to our night quarters, and there we slept as soundly as possible (nine in the two.rooms), with the windows open and the fires burning. There are two pails of fresh milk, which seme.drink neat and others prefer to take mixed with a little whisky before turning in. Some fall asleep at once, ethers not so soon, the American doctor's cheery ringing laugh ',sounding long on the quiet night air, as he and.thecommander tell alternately the most astounding yarns, .each ;with a clenountent more startling than the Last. In the. silent Pauses between the tales, while they are collecting their wits, we can hear the croaking of the frogs awayinthe distance on the borders of the marsh, and witht these two sounds alternately ringing in our ears we fell asleep." There is considerable literary ability in their deserip- tion of a native "Korrobboree " :--"The sound of , a lamb's bleat reminded one also of England, where teeday is the longest day, though here it is the shortest ;in the year. The sky is leaden, and, though there is; no frost, there is a feel about the clear air like a black winter. After dinner, which was at 6 p.m., we went:to .see .9, korrobboree, where the black-fellows were .encamped at a short distance from the house. There were twatribes of these, and about 200 of them in aIL They werepainted with white and black streak across the face and chest, and got up in correct style with skins and spears and boomerangs, and lay the light of the fusee Which were ,kindled in cireb around they looked sufficiently ;hideous. The tribeatdanced alternately, and the watch- words of their songs ;appeared to-be half reiglish,Jialf ea-tivo.. A great deal of the action of the dance consisted

in striking- the ground at the same moment.soas to .cause an echoing thud with their feet. One of the :re- peated actions was to .cause the muscles of the deg and nigh to quiver simultmeouslv from toe to stamaCh mat most extraordinary nmaner. At the end of each tgure they brought themeehresap sharp with a straafge, deep- toned sound, half hurrahamlf grunt, " Wir—r—r—wuhr .hey would then wheel rright across the inclosed space' •in line, and chattering as; fast as they could, upon the NVOIXten who were sitting,antthe grounct-and also sing- ing,e,sort of chorus of a few notes; the-line would then Iwheetback, break up into twee and threes, brandishing theirxhort sticks and clubs over their heads, each man vociferating quickly to his mate, and then all of a fud- den these incoherent sounds woald all coalesce together into a.chorus, and the band,.again united, would cause the ground once more to vibmtele the reiteratedeadenee .of theiratamp." The natimality of the young Priaces breaks forth in •many ,a;sfmty expression. They .evidently love their .eauntre..and are proud of their,acamtrymen. They say of the gainers at a copper minothay visited:—" All here .oncandall,;are true Cornishmen, fine stalwart fellows; most of those we see young, tall, aarthroad, with a slight South Austmlian drawl, but of the raelEnglish bone and sinew and ...straightforward leok about their faces." Seotchmen vllJ read the following with pride :—"The Scotch are-the hest and most anecessfill of emigrants. Half the most ;prominent among the statesmen of the Canadian Confederation of QueenelantLaad Victoria are born Beots, and 41 the great merchants of India are of , the same nation. Whether it is that the Scotch emi- grants are for the most part men of 'better education than those of other nations, or whether the Scotchman owes his uniform sixcess in every climate -to ,his perse- verance or his shrewdness, the fact remains that wher- ever abroad you come across a Scotchman youlavariably find him prosperees and respected in cOeulating contentment ; and with a strong-handed, open- hearted hospitality that no words can render adequate thanks for. To come in contact only with such colonists is riarally healthgiving." That Log- and is their standard the following extract shows:— "From the summit of .11fekunt Lofty are many beautiful views, one especially from the Eagle Nest Inn down Waterfall Valley, looking back on Adelaide and the sea In the distance. The hills hero are all covered with trees to the summits, and reminded us of the blue mountains in Jamaica. • But about everything—the hedgerows, the fields, the grass, the carts, the men, these last stalwart, and brown, and unexcitable—there was an umistakable stamp of England."

The following humorous incident is too good to be omitted :—" A couple of miles outside Angaston a caval- cade of oddfellows, with sashes and bows, came forth to meet us. One of them was brandishing his red ban- ner on high, which operation, as neither he nor his horse I were used to it, caused the two to part company, the man being shot in one direction and the banner in the other. We picked him up and put him into one of the carriages, and carried him back to a public-house at the entrance of the village from which he had started. This VMS his home, and here we left him, a little stunned and bruised, but no doubt able, after further slight re- freshment, to feel quite himself again." Turning to more serious matters, we will conclude with two extracts, one prophetic and the other pathetic. The first shows that the spirit which Australia has ex- hibited in her recent patriotic offers is no momentary enthusiasm. At Adelaide, the diary says, on June 18th—" We went to the opening of the National Art Gallery in the new University Buildings, to which the Queen has lent some pictures from Windsor. Chief Jus- tice Way did the honours. One hundred members of the Volunteer Force (of which there are in all 1,500) were drawn up at the side, under Major Fergusson, and looked very well in their scarlet uniforms. These men volunteered to go to the Transvaal, and meant it too, but were declined. South Australia evidently considers itself a real and living portion of the British Empire, and is quite willing to share the burdens of Citizenship with the mother country." Our last extract will show that their mother's kindness of heart has not been with- out its influence on the young princes. "In the after- noon drove to the Hospital for Incurables, where there are about forty-eight patients; we went all over it and saw all in every ward. There were several poor boys with spinal affections, one very bright little chap chatted with us some time and gave us some carving of his own doing. There were also some P6or paralysed old men who were sunning themselves in front. We had a quiet dinner at .Government House, and afterwards some music and hymns with Lady and Miss Jervois in the drawing-room.

VOLUNTARS SCHOOLS AND THE Enuceporr ACT.—Ort Monday a deputation from the National Society and from various educational bodies in Liverpool had an interview at the Education Department with Lord Carlingford, the Lord President of the Privy Council, and the Right Hon. A J Mundella, M.P.—Mr Paget, M.P., stated that the object of the deputations, in which the managers and teachers of all voluntary schools concurred, was to urge the abolition or mrdification of article 114 of the Education Code, which was known as the 17s 61 limitation, and contended that it operated against both efficiency an economy, and was especially prejudicial to the best of the schools in poor die- tricts.—Mr Mundella said the 17s 81 clause had been intro- duced by Lord Sindon expressly in the interests of denominational schools ; and since then their subscriptions had not increased but diminished, whilst the !ncressed cost per head of educating the children had been more than met by larger grants under the code, so that there were already a number of Church of England and other voluntary schools self-supporting. The expenditure of voluntary school managers had since 1878 increased from is 8d to Ss 4d per child, whereas the grants had increased 3s Id and the schools teeslid per head.

The question Lis, to some ex- ttant, mysterione, many and varied cases without satis- factory cause being assigned for their occurrence; and •it is, therefore, -to be hoped that some light will be -thrown upon the matter, which is one ,osver7 consider- able importance to all farmers, but mere particularly Ito those who bread high-class and pedigree stock. • EXPBRIMENTS vx ENSILAGB IN CILBSIIIRIL—A few 'weeks ago the Corporation of Crewe instructed the manager of the sewage farm to test the reriative value of ,eosilage and hay in 'feeding milking cattle, and on qatur- day the following statement was issued Two milking COBS fed with ensilage consumed in two weeks 1,1301 b .of ensilage (41113 per -day each), which at Rd. per cwt. cost-Is. 6d.; 3121 b of hay, at 3s. per cwt.., Ss, 441. ; 68115 of tuniips, 5d.; 168th of oats, at 3s. per busbal,llos. How To •Iltrr A Horan—Au did horseman sayik--df • you want teinly a horse don'ttelieve your own brother.; take no man's word for it; your eye is your market. Don't buy a 'horse in buses& lir/itch him and take everything off but his halter, and head him around. If . he has a corn, or is stiff, or has any other failing, you can see it. Let him go by himself always, and if he staves right into anything you know be is blind. No matter how clear and bright his eyes are, he can't see any. more than a bat. Back him, too. Come horses show their weakness at tificks in that way when they don't in any other; but, be as smart as you can, yeu'll get caught sometimes. Even an expert gets stuck. A horse may look ever so nice and go a great pace and yet have fits. There isn't a man could tell it till something happens; or he may have a weak back. Give him the whip and off he goes for a mile or twp, then all of a sudden he i stops n the road. After a rest he starts again, but he soon stops for good, and nothing but a derrick can move him. The weak points of a horse can be better dis- covered while standing than while moving. If he is sound he will stand firmly and squarely On his Ihnba without moving them, feet flatly upon the ground, with legs plump and naturally poised; or if the foot is lifted from the ground and the weight taken from it, disease may be suspected, or at least tenderness, which is a pre- rursor 'of disease. It the horse stands with his feet spread apart or straddles with his hind legs, there is a weakness in the loins and the kidneys are disordered. Heavy pulling bends the knees. Bluish, milky, cast eyes in hores indicate moon blindness or something else. A bad tempered one keeps his ears thrown back; a kick- ing horse is apt to have scarred legs; a stumbling horse has blemished knees. When the skin is rough and harsh, and does not move easily to the touch, the horse is a heavy eater and digestion is bad. Never buy a horse whose breathing organs are at all impaired. Place your ear at the heart, and if a wheezing sound is heard it is an indication of trouble.

NORTH AND liOl2T-illiA-ST LANCASHIRE RURAL NO'TES.— A North-East Lancashire correspondent writes :—On Wednesday week, while the sun was shining, I heard a throstle in full song, though the ground was deeply covered with frozen snow. The sparrows, starlings, and rooks have taken the change of weather seemingly as a matter of course. Their movements indicatedt hat they did not expect the storm to be of loaf duration, and on the mea- dows and slopes the sun quickly melted great patches of snow, which enabled them to get a sufficiency of food. Rooks, starlings, sparrows, and other small birds, have been quite numerous all winter. Usually'nlost of the starlings leave us during the dead winter months' but this and last winter (which was much milder than this) nearly all the starlings have remained with us, and they were in full song and pairing (as were also the fussy and noisy sparrows) before the snow-storm on Tuesday week. The larks returned with the lapwings, and were in song on the uplands and moors the same day that the lapwings arrived. When the snow com- menced to fall, the peewits and larks cleared out from the moors, and they are now again in the lower and more sheltered grounds, or at the seaside, between the estuaries of the Ribble and Wyre.— Another correspondent writes :—I hear from various quarters good reports of the pro gress of the lambing season. The lambs are not only numerous, but both they and the dams are doing well, with very few losses. I still hear serious accounts about abortion in cattle.- A , few days ago I was in the Garstang district and was told of an instance of a farmer there having as many as thirty cows which have " pioked." It has been sug- gested that some of these cases of abortion may be due, first, to the offensive smells in the shippon arising from the kind of food upon which the cattle have been fed, and again, to /he want of ventilation and the absence of any effort to'keep down the smells, as, for instance, using fresh soil in the shippon. The few days' frost were turned to account to get rid of all the surplus dressings of fences by burning them. Much produce has been forced into the market. The stock of turnips is now getting low,but there is still a great quantity of potatoes on hand, and some of the farmers will have to make a push to get their stocks cleared before new ones come up., In ,the district which supplies the Garstang market with potatoes, magnums will be chiefly planted—few if any, champions; there will be some Reading Heroes, Pater- sons, and some of the newer kinds. There is no ap- parent sign of any ditninution of area to be planted,at I being felt that the four-course system of cropping does not admit of any lessening of the area for potato crop- ping. The low price of wheat has induced many to tate a crop of oats in place of wheat. Farmers are becoming anxious to get into the land. The wet is not so bad hire as is reported in some parts of England.
Public Analysts have submitted CADI3URY'S COCOA to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt.

div.head: DEATH OF HONEST 'TOM.
div.p: DEATH OF HONEST 'TOM.

I All interested in horse breeding mill, we are sure, re- gret to leer of the death of Honest Tom (1105), the pro- pasty of T. H. Miller, Esq., of Singleton Park. Old Tom 'died on Wednesday, in his loose box at the Park stables. lEe has been ill lately, and has been treated by able veterinary surgeons, but he was beyond recovery and ,died as stated, much to the regret of this owner and the staff engaged at the stables. Up to recently he was in full possession of his health and vigour, which was (considered a very, remarkable circumstance when it is zemembered that in early life he was in a highly fed con- dition. He proved himself one of the finest sires in the kingdom, and earned national distinctions. He had a :remarkably sound constitution,and he transmitted to ,his offspring, especially those out of good brood mares, his wonderful characteristics. It is an easy matter to pick out at our district shows his progeny which have secured an envied repute both in Britain and America. Honest Tom was a beautiful bay, stood 14 hands, and weighed .a ton. He was bred by Mr. Wm. .Welcher, in the South, and his old owner purposely came over to seethe veteran during the great sale of horses at Single- ton Park in August last. Honest Toin was then in his box, and had during the whole day crowds of ad- mirers. Ile was first brought into the show ring at Bury-Stadmunds in 1887, and he easily won the first card. Me followed up his success in a most brilliant tanner. He carried off six Royal first ,prizes in suc- cession, at:Leicester 1888, Manchester 1869, Oxford 1870, Wolverhampton 1871, and Cardiff 1872, When he finally retired, covered with his distinguishedhonours, from the show ring for the stud, having won prizes to the value of over 4520. In the year 1871 the Fylde Horsebreeding Compauy, whose most useful operations have made the Fylde sue of the best breeding districts for Shire horses in the kingdorn,.purchased Honest Tom for'soogs., and at the 'breaking up of the company's establishment in 1878 he was purchased by Mr. Miller for that sum. Ho proved quite a ,mine of wealth to the breeders in the Fylde, for up .to the period of his going into the district about £.1.5 was the,full price for a foal at weaning time; but soon the value of his foals were made known, and from E5O ,to IEIOO has not been an uncommon price, whilst his yearlings and two-year-olds have made as much as from £3ooto eBOO. Honest Toms have been sent to all parts of the globe, and at the agricultural shows in the county special prizes have been given for his off- spring. This splendidkorse was of the Old Cambridge- shire and Lincolnshire Fen blood, his pedigree tracing far back into the last ..eentury, through a long list of noted sires of their day, and his being in-bred through both sire and dam to an 'unusually famous sire of nearly fifty years .ago (Seward's Major) who traced back to Wiseman 's Honest Tom, foaled in 1800, made Honest Tom a famous sire—a sire that so put the stamp of size, substance, constitution, quality, and good looks upon his deseendants that they are easily re- cognised. During the last eleven years, not a Royal or county show has passed but some of his progeny have been among fife prize-winners. At the first London Cart Horse Show in 1880, held under the auspice i Of the English Cart Horse Society, Ids stock were the most auccessful winners, and his son Admiral, the champion I stallion of the show; after winning two Royals (first at )erby, 1881, and first at Reading. 1882) was sold at a tang price to .go to Australia, where, soon after landing„, he was sold by auction for £l,BOO. For the past few seasons Mr. Miller kept Honest Tom principally for use in his own stud. The old horse died on the very day wben. some of his deseehdants were being exhibited with success at the great exhibition. of Shire Horses at the Agricultural Hall, Islington, a report sf which will be fouad its another column.

div.head: . THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: . THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

THE PARIS POULTRY SHOW. In saying aught respecting the Show of Poultry at Paris, it is needful to point out that there is one great difference between those held in France and the ma- jority of shows which take place in this country,. Here they are supported by fanciers most of all, which fan- ciers are in the greater number of instances breeders who have only a small amount of space at their dis- ,posal, and who regard the pursuit as a hobby, a source of pleasure. In most cases they wish it to pay, so as not to be a tax on their pockets, and the exhibition of birds is in many cases simply for the purpose of testing the; correctness of their breeding, and as an advertise- ment of their stock. Were it not for this latter reason many fanciers would not exhibit at all. The winner of a first prize at any of our great shows has the prices he can obtain for birds or eggs considerably enhanced, and if he be fortunate enough to win a cup at the Crystal Palace or Birmingham, he has, for one year at any rate, possession of a Fortunatus purse. Many good breeders, it is true, pay no attention in the buying of stock birds to prize winning. They can form their own judgment as to the merits of fowlS. But with the majority the winning of 'a prize is a hall mark, and for a fowl so stamped they are willing to pay a good price, varied by the length of their purse§ and the prizes won. To "the fancy," as such, we are indebted for the pre- servation of many breeds, and for the introduction of others. Without it we fear the poultry question in England would have been in a much worse condition than it now is. Therefore, though the direct influence' upon the agricultural interest has not been great, the indirect benefit, by preservation of races and breeds, has been simply incalculable. In war, the man or men who hold a position, perhaps against fearful odds, and thus covers the advance or retreat of an army, has done a very great service, and this is what "the fancy" has done for poultry. Farmers have now a choice of breeds and a knowledge of their qualities and characteristics which could only have been obtained by specialists, and i their advantages n this way are enormous.. Some day fanciers may be less numerous, but we do not think this will ever be so under ordinary conditions, for the Eng- lish are a' race of breeders, and our much maligned climate offers facilities not found elsewhere. In France the case is: altogether different. There, in some districts at least, such as the departments of La Sarth, Auge, Seine-et-Oise, &c., poultry breeding is car- ried on to an enormous extent. Small farms are the rule there, and poultry breeding one of their most im- portant sources of income. Every farm has its stook of pure bred poultry, and whilst the same care as to feather and markings is not taken as in England, general princi- ples are regarded, and no deviation from the recognised type is sanctioned. There is much less cross-breeding in France than in England, and the purity of the races is sustained. One advantage of tho system is, there is not the temptation to in-breeding or the introduction of foreign blood that British breeders often have, to a large' extent the breed of the district only is kept. Around Houda.n, we find the fowl of that name almost universal. In one part of La Sarthe there are the La Fleche, in another Du Mans. In the Auge district of Normandy the Creve-Cceur is universal. Thus fresh blood is easily obtained, in all places the economic qualities' of. their special varieties are carefully maintained, and'a fowl or family which does not fulfil on the table or in the egg basket the promise made, is the wastea, not the speci- men with A few wrong coloured feathork in his breast, or is deficient in foot plumage. To this we may attribute the great superiority of the French poultry. The show at Paris, held recently, exhibits the fact that whilst in that country the economic Side of the poultry question is regarded as the most important, the ordinary poultry keepers are not the exhibitors. Out of the more than 1,200 pens of poultry in the Palais Plndustrie, which (as there were from four to six hens shown' in one pen) means about 3,000 birds, quite two- thirds were shown by some six or eight exhibitors— these the. great French poultry dealers. One of these (M. Lernome,.of Crosne) had 210 pens, or upwards, of 800 birds, himself. Whether the same thing is found in the district shows of France we are unable to say, but we hope to visit some of them next season' when it will be possible to form a better' idea of it. At Paris the fact mentioned above has always .been apparent, and

this yettiVvas more evident than ever. It is a regretable 4 fact, for rre do not take it as a healthy sign when dealerS take off all the prizes. They prevent others exhibiting, and if it:ls at all a general rule in France, probably ere long it Will be necessary to introduce more restrictions than have been already imposed, in order, to check the great exhibitors. This has been necessary in British shows. At the Paris show in most of the classes an ex- hibitor can Only send four pens, but as no entry fee is charged and the prizes are liberal, many lots Fe sent that would never be in a show pen were the prizes they might gain the only inducement But the show is very largely a market, and the owners of the fowls are per- mitted to sell them for delivery at the close oi the show in the show itself. It is not even necessary to record the sale with the authorities, who derive no benefit from the sales. At the show, as might have been expected, theative breeds mustered very well indeed, and we never, even at. Paris, saw such a magnificent collection. No one having web it can deny that .the French have brought the breeding of poultry to a very high pitch of perfec- tion. Of the whole we thought the La Fleche variety the best, and we wished that this breed could be thor- oughly acclimatised here, as it is one of the finest for table purposes that is known. Crevek were also good, as were La Bresse, though the latter are never so good looking alive as dead. Houdans were deficient in size and qaulity, the same forces at work in the English Houdan evidently acting iir France. The other French races were well repraseted, and all this section of the show was very interesting. The Prix d' honneur, as the great prize is called, for the section, was awarded to La Flecne. The foreign section was noticeable as showing the growth of a fancy in France. Cochins and Polish, the latter of which are known as Hollandaise on the Conti- nent, are the most popular, and there welt some really good specimens exhibted. Of course, there is nothing like the English Cochin mania of thirty years ago, but it is not a little remarkable that Cochms should be so popular in France. Many other British breeds were present, but deserve no special mention. Turkeys were good, but geese and ducks not like what we have at home, though a line lot of Rouen ducks was the Prix d' honneur for this section. The show of dead poultry was a very fine one, but not quite so large as that of last year. It presented no new features over those mentioned then by us in this column. SEASONABLE HINTS. We are now at the end of the show season, and breeders have other work in hand. Even Bantam breeders have begun to mate up their pens, and all who intend to have any chickens should lose no time in getting the yai•da together. Some one must always be latt, but there is no need for any one to be late, and, therefore, every one who has not "put up" the breeders should do so without delay. Next month and the early part of April are the great times for hatching laying birds, and there is no time to be lost in order to secure these.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

Owing to the snow and rain, the soil at the present time is in the worst possible condition to deal with, and no attempt should be made to interfere with it now. We must wait for the water to drain away, when we may expect to find the soil in good order. The frosts that have visited us at intervals have disintegrated the most obstinate clods, so that when the land becomes sufficiently dry: it cannot fail to work like ashes, and provide an agreeable seed bed. During the frost and snow of the past week the birds have been extremely troublesome to the buds of gooseberries and currants, but their mischievous raids were arrested by the appli- cation of lime and soot dusted over the branches when moist from the thaw which took place, most of the days, about 11 a.m. The rain has,however, washed nearly all the soot and lime away, and another dressing must be given, so as to make the buds distasteful. We also in- tend to stretch black cotton in various directions over the trees. This the birds cannot see in their swift flight, and when they come in contact with it they are shy in returning for a time.

SHLECT Vearrriaties.—Parmips.—Of these there are only two sorts usually grown, the Hollow-Crowned and the Student, and either of them will' do.—Radishes may be represented by the Olive-shaped, Long Scarlet, Short Top, and the White and Bed Turnip sorts.—. Par- sley, though rather a common article in daily use, is fre- quently supplied indifferently, if the best curled variety is not asked for. The flavour of all are alike, but the market value bears no comparison.—Brocedi.—Wal- cheran or Early White Cape, for early autumn supply; Dilcocles Bride and Knight's Protecting follow; and Cattell's Eclipse will continue the succession till the end of May. It is a matter of surprise to us that the class of autumn and winter vegetables is not more largely grown.—Cautiflowers.—Most people who liave a garden are acquainted with Veitch's Autumn Giant, which is , the best vegetable of its class ever introduced. During this season it has been in good form in many gardens up till Christmas. For spring or early summer, ,Early Lon- don is perhaps the best, and is usually sown in autumn for the first batch.—Tarnips.—Early Purple Munich is the earliest of all. This may be succeeded by Early Snowball, and as a hardy winter sort few, if any, will surpass Veitch's Red Globe. Those who prefer a yellow kind should procure Troughton's Preston Yellow.— Potatoes.—Any of the variety of Ashleaf are good for the early crops, and Lapstone is a good second early. Magnum Bonum is a great favourite :as a late one. The best-flavoured late potato we have tried this season has been the old Scotch Regent , Tim FaoIT GARDEN.—Primroses: The garden varie- ties as well as the common one have been in flower more or lass during the winter, and we noticed a row of the latter under a hedge in a cottage garden looking quite fresh not many hours after the frost and snow of last week. had disappeared. Every cottager should have a few of the improved varieties in his front garden, and by saving seeds from them the number of varieties may be still Increased. The planting of them may be performed I any time during the next two or three weeks, but the best time is early autumn, so that the plants may esta- blish themselves ready for the spring campaign. Those who have not taken up their culture will gain a season by commencing at once, for the plants are sure to flower and pitoduce seeds this season. In planting they ahould be arranged near the outer side of the beds or borders so that they may not be obscured by the presence of.taller plants. As they come in flower they should be num- bered, and opposite a corresponding number written in the pocket-book there should be a description of the flower such as will remind the owner of theCcolour of each, so as to facilitate their arrangement at any future time. Those who have not secured , a number_of Rose Stocks should do so at once if they intend: to do any budding during the summer. The dog rose, such as , grows In the hedges is the one used for this purpose. All strong roots that may be attached to them are removed close to the stem, and all the side shoots are cut in a similar manner, so that they have the appearance of walking sticks with a large knob at the encl. Tme,Wninow.—Hyacinths, whether in pots or glasses will needcareful watching, as they are likely to be drawn up weakly if they are not supplied with sufficient i air. If the foliage gets n advance of the flower it is a sure sign that more air is required, but cold currents must at all times be avoided. As the flower spike, ad- vances give the pot a slight turn round daily, or it will be inclined to one side—a mistake that is not easily rec- tified even when the stakes are put to them. Never allow them to get dry, and feed them with liquid stimu- lants (weak at first) or apply Clay's fertiliser to the sur- face of the soil.

ATTEMPTED WILDER AND SIIICIDE.—A married man named James Pickard, living apart from his wife, has been paying his attentions to a domestic servant, at Leeds, named Gilbert. She, learning that her lover bad a wife living, desired that the intimacy might ce3Be. Tkis ren- dered Pickard furious, and on Friday night he went to where Gilbert was in service and discharged a revolver at her, just missing her head. She escaped, and he then shot a hole in the roof of his own mouth. He was taken to the Infirmary. INTEMPERANCE am PAUDERISII.—On Saturday, in Lon- don, a conference of relieving officers of the metropolis was held to consider the relation of intemperance to pauperism. The conference,which was called by the National Temperance League, was presided over by Mr Samuel Morley, M.P., who said that on his retirement from Parliamentary life at the next diesolution, he intended devoting his energies to press- ing upon the people the importance of temperance habits. If the £126,000,000 now spent upon intexicating drink were reduced by £100,000,000, ere long not a loom in the country would be standing idie.—The conference was addressed by relieving officers, who all testified to the distinct connection between drink and pauperism and between drink and lunacy. Intemperance, it was stated by several, was not so much the result of bad homes, but the latter were made wretched by the habits of the people who dwelt in them. Testimony WaS also borne to the circumstance that very few of the applicants for relief were abstainers. A RING'S WORKSHOP —ln a letter recently received from Burrnah a characteristic sketch is given in illustration of the state of the country under its present ruler, in which it is stated that at S ce'sine there is what is called the king's workshop, which was erected at the instance of the last ruler at an enormous expense, his idea being to build steamers for his own and the country's use. The shipbuild- ing yard is at Mandalay, and the place at Sagine was designed as a foundry, in which cast and wrought iron was to be treated. Two large furnaces, 15 boilers, three furnaces for cast iron, seven large engines, five rolling mills for bar iron, and a quantity of other machinery (including a large steam hammer, lathes, punching and shearing machines, and stone and ore crushers) have been put down. All that is required is to start the fires and raise steam ; yet this valuable property is meantime overgrown with the pro- ducts of the soil. The large steam hammer is twined round with beautiful crimson creepers ; from out of one of the furnaces grows a large prickly cactus; the rolling mills are shaded with large tree ferns. The machinery, however, is not rusted, though nearly ten years have elapsed since the last king died. The works were suspended at his death, and the present king will neither spend more money on the undertaking nor sell it to others.—lron. KAY'S TIC PILLS, a specifie in Neuralgia. Pace ache, an. 93. The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. SUNDAY CLOSING—The Earl of Derby presented peti- tions from inhabitente of Manchester, Itawtenstall, Earles- town, Hollinwood, and Droylsden in favour of Sunday clos- ing. Tng WAR RAILWAY—The Under Secretary for War was questioned in the House of Lords last night as to the pro- posed line of railway from Suakim to Berber.—Lord Mom- LEY stated that there were two or three engineering difficul- ties to face, but there was no insuperable difficulty in the way of the construction of the line, and it was believed that a portion sufficient for military purposes, if not the whole of the line, might be constructed before the autumn set in. Referring to the announcement Lord Wolseley is reported to have made of his intention to advance on and take Khar- toum, Lord Morley said the Government bad no information on the subject.—Lord SALISBURY thought the railway scheme had rather an "Arabian Nights " air about it, and that the proposal would rather alarm some of our most distinguished railway authorities.— Lord GRANVILLE replied that all the plant was perfectly ready when the arrangement was made, that the line would be what was known as a contractor's railway, that its primary object was of a military character, and that lines of this character could be constructed much more rapidly than an ordinary line.—Lord NAPIER OF DI AGDALA, alluding to the suggestion that terms might be made with the Mandi, said he had never shown any disposition to treat, and we should either have to beat him or let him alone. Their lordships adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tutraseemr. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. MHE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN.—Lord HARTINGTON gave an assurance that there was no foundation for the statement that a proposal had been made to organin a force of 5,000 Zulus to proceed to the Soudan. A proposal had, however, been received from the Lieutenant Governor of Natal offer- ing to organise a corps of natives of that colony. Until the Government received further information of the progress of affairs in South Africa he could not say whether it was possible to take advantage of any of the offers which had been made. The noble Marquis was quest•oned as to what would be done with the diaries of General Gordon, end re- plied that if they were like that of Colonel Stewart, which WAS a sort of substitute for despatches, they would be prin- ted in the same way as other public docaments ; but if they I appeared to he of a private character the wishes of the rela- tives and friends of the late General Gordon would have to be consulted. In reply to another question, Lord HARTINGTON said there would be an increase in the army beyond the 3,000 men taken in the Supplementary Estimates, but he could not say whether to the extent of 15,000 or any other number.—Sir H. TYLER expressed a desire that a request should be forwarded to Lord Wolseley for the text of the speech be re cently made to troops of General Gordon at Korti, but was told by Lord HARTING• TON that the Government had full confidence in the manner lin which Lord Wolseley had carried out and would carry out his instructions.
FOREIGN NEWS.

Mr Anderson, M.P. for Glasgow, has received the colonial appointment of Master of the Melbourne Mint. Tax LORD MAYOR OF Dummr.—The Secretary of the 'Fitzgerald Testimonial Committee telegraphed to the Lord Mayor of Dublin, on Thursday, that his subscription would be returned, consequent upon his 'mean and abject apology" regardiag the lbyal visit. Representatives of the Church of England Temperance Society had a conference on Thursday with a number of members of Parliament, and it is understood that a bill will be formally introduced within the next two or three weeks for the establishment of district licensing boards. WORKING-CLASS REPRESENTATION.—At Birmingham, OD Thursday, the miners' conference passed a resolution that it was not only desirable, but imperative, that newly-enfran- chised working-classes should use their political power to return representatives to Parliament of their own class, to help legislation affecting their interest, and to make the House of Commons truly representative. Mils. WELDON Aomx.—Mrs Weldon obtained another victo-y on Thursday. Last Tune she obtained judgment against Dr Semple for £l,OOO damages for libel. Dr Semple obtained a rule nisi for a new trial, and the hearing of the motion was set down for Thursday morning. Dr Semple, however, was not represented, and, on Mrs Weldon's applica- tion, the rule was dismissed with costa. I KAY'S COMPOUND, a demulcent anodyne, expectorant, for Coughs and Cads.
