THE AFGHAN PRONTIER.—SevaraI questions Were pro- posed in reference to the Afghan frontier, and to these the PRIME MINISTER replied that at the present moment ques- tions relating to policy sr to contingencies in the future on the subject of 'the Afghan frontier were, in the judg- ment of the Government, prejudicial to the public in- terest. _ .

SLIPPLT.—In Committee of Supply, on the Supplemen- tary Naval Estimates, Sir T. BEASSEY moved a vote of £330,000 to defray the expenditure for a naval force arising out of the military operations in Egypt—Mr. LADOIICHERE moved the redaction of the vote by £250,000, contending that the money ought to be charged upon the Egyptian Government.—Upon a division the amendment was nega- tived by 66 to 22. Several votes for the civil services and revenue departments were also agreed to. Progress was then reported, and the House resumed. THE INDILN CONTINGENT IN THE SOIMLN.—Mr. J. K. CROSS formally moved a resolution providing that the or- dinary pay of the Indian troops to be employed in the Soudan as well as the ordinary charges of any vessels be- longing to the Government of India may be employed in the

- RETIREMENT OF GENERAL BRACKENBURY'S FORCE. TORTS. SUNDAY —News is hourly expected here from General Brackenbury's force. ,Great difficulty, however, is experienced in inducing messengers to carry despatches, the destruction of property by British troops having caused a feeling of intense hostility on the part of the tribes between thia place and Abu Hamed. Some time may consequently elapse before intelligence of General Brackenbury's force is received. The Mufti'. of Dongota has received intelligence that his troops, which are encamped at Daginzet,near Ham- dab, have made a reconnaissance in the desert as far as the Koa Wells, which were found to be destroyed. They con- tinued scouting to Keren, but finding no enemy commenced ' to return. The enemy, however, overtook them, and a short engagement ensued, the rebels being eventually forced to re- treat. The Isiss on the Mudir's side was three men wounded and three missing. The enemy being mounted on camels were able to carry off their dead. Two Arab merchants who have arrived here report that they left Berber twenty days ago. They say that at that time the fighting force there bad evacuated the town, and hail crossed to the right bank of the river to opposite the English. They say that the reading of the Koran is now forbidden to the people, who are crdered to read only the filabeli's books. The Mah- di has issued instructions that his troops are not to charge the English, but are to fight them at a distance. If they do this, he tells them that God ac ill destroy their enemies. KORTI, MONDAY.—The plan of advance against Abu limed has been abandoned. General Brackenbury has re- ceived orders not to proceed any further with his column, but to retire for a general concentration of the force. The three men of the Mudirs' troops who were reported to have been taken prisoners in the skirmish with marauding Arabs turn out to have deserted. They have since been recaptured. —Standard. From General Lord Wolseley : KORTI, TUESDAY, 5-10 P.M —General Brackenbury's force is now returning to Merawi. It reached Berti on the let inst. KORTI, WEDNESDAY, 6-40 r.m —News has reached here of the arrival of General Brackenbury's column near Owli 'eland without molestation. Several rapids are now dan- gerous for whalers descending, but those of Endermi have been passed without loss of life. Six boats, however, were wrecked. ltfo•t of the troops are marching along the banks, only the necessary crews for navigation being left on board with the voyayeurs. A convoy with the last of the wounded arrived here to-day; all are progressing favourably. ARRIVAL OF GENERAL BULLER AT KORTI. • / Koun,Sunrna.v.—Geoeral Buller has arrived from Gak- dul Wells. Lord Wolseley to-day addressed the late General Gordon's black troops, praising them for their gallantry and loyalty to Gordoa. His Lordship specially enlogieed the conduct of the engineer and native officer coin- , mending the steamer on which Sir Charles Wilson and party embarked for Khartoum. Lord Welseley promised to pay all sums due to the troops, and to provide them with new clothing as soon as possible. He also declared that he would recognise all General Gordon's promises. It is repor- ted that a small body af marauders have attacked a British convoy, composed of men of the Kabbabish tribe, while on the way to the wells near Hovreiyatt, killing 12 of their number. Roan, SUNDAY.—AII the sick• and Founded have left, Gakdul. Of the convoy which reached Kceti to-day several men apparently suffered much from the heat. The sur- geons in charge marched all the way, giving the camels to the patients. The remainder of the troops will withdraw from Gakdul gradually, spoiling the wells as they retire. Most will probably have to trudge on foot, the available camels being required to carry the supplies. The water at the Howeiyatt Wells is running so short that pore with reserve tanks have been established 20 and 30 miles out from here.—Daily Neve. Komi, WEDNESDAY. The last convoy of sick and wounded from Gakdul, numbering 110, under the care of Surgeon-Major Conolly, arrived Lere to-day. Captain Walsh, Captain Pagett and Quartermaster Jamieson are doing well. Davidson and Surgeon Turner are suffering from dysentery. Seven men died on the journey. The remainder of General Gordon's troops which came in the steamers from Khartoum have also arrived here. They number, with women and children, 113. Surgeon Major Conolly reports that the road from Galvinl is open, but small gangs a/ robbers are on the lookout for booty. _ THE SUAKIIVI EXPEDITION. Cam% BllNDAY.—General Graham will not leave here before March 9th. Major-General Sir G. Greaves left tor •Suakim this morning. CAIRO, Molmmr.—Prince Hassan left here this morning for the Soudan. BOMBAY. MONDAY.—The last detachment of Indian troops for services in Egypt sailed to-day for Suakim. SUAKIN, SATURDAY.—MS hired transport Geelong, after disembarking the remainder of the East Surrey Regiment, which has joined the cainp, will sail at day-break to-mor- row. Lieutenant W. B. Askwith, of the Royal Engineers, who was killed yesterday by the accidental explosion of a mine, was buried to-day in the English cemetery with mili- tary honours. SUAKIN, TUESDAY.—A rebel spy coming into Suakim was shot by the sentry. A portion of the Sikhs hsve disem- barked. The remainder will land this evening. ARRIVAL OF INDIAN TROOPS AT SUAKIM.

SIIAKTM, Turmsnav—Major-General Sir G Greaves, chief I of General Graham's staff, landed here from the troopship Humber to-day. Measures bat% been taken to prevent the nightly wrecking of the advanced redoubts by the rebels. Brigadier General Hudson, commander of the- Indian con- tingent, together with his staff and a portion of the 17th Bengal Native Infantry, arrived here to-day on board the Indian Government steamer Clive. DEFEAT OF THE EGYPTIAN GARRI- SON AT KASSALA. The intelligence of the disaster to the Kassala garrison was received with some surprise in London. The successful sortie which they made on the occasion of the arrival of a provision convoy near that city must have taken place only a day or two before the disaster occurred which is now chronicled, although in reports of that engagement no data was given. The Hadendowast who were then the opposing force, were variously said to have lost from 2,000 to 3,500 men. No details have been received of the engagement in which the garrison was last involved, but it appears that on the 2nd February the garrison made a sortie as far as Kol- eta, and there again met an apparently large body of tribes- men under the Mandi's standard. An engagement took Ow, and the Egyptian soldiers were compelled to retire with the enormous loss of 28 officers and 872 men which, after the severe struggle in which the garrison had en- gaged during the past year, must have represented about a third of the Governor's regular force. THE NEW EXPEDITION. The hired transport Norfolk left Millwall Docks on Mon- day with 2,000 tons of railway sleepers, three locomotives and tenders, ,ke, for Suakim. The transport &roma has left Woolwich with 1,500 tons of commissariat stores; and the transport Amethyst sailed from London Docks on Saturday with 800 tons of ice and refrigerators for the supply of the base hospital of Suakim. Up to Saturday seventy transports had been chartered by the Government for the new expe- dition. The War Office authorities have given a contract for steam engines for pumping water and for the supply of the first fzlty miles of pipes far the conveyance of water from Suakim to General Graham's advanced position, to an American firm, whose chief, Mr. Tweddle, is now engaged, with the proviso that the pipes are to be English manufac- tured. DEPARTURE OF AUSTRALIAN TROOPS.
WAR ESTIMATE.

SYDNRY, TUESDAY.—To-day was observed as a public holiday in celebration of the departure of the New South Wales contingent for the Soudan. Since the date on which the colony's offer was accepted to the departure of troops, public enthusiasm has been maintained at its utmost ten- sion. The number of volunteers has reached six times the required strength, and the Patriotic Fend amounts to £45,000. The troops were reviewed on Saturday by Lord Augustus Loftus, Governor of New South %Vales. On Sun- day special services were held in Anglican and Roman Cathedrkls' and to-day the popular enthusiasm was un- bounded. On reaching the quay the men formed square, and were addressed by the Governor, who said: The eyes of your gracious Queen will be bent upon your exertions, and in every part of the world where our flag floats, men, women, and children will eagerly read of your exploits and pray for your success. You are doing this to shoe to the world the unity of the mighty and invincible Empire of which you are members.—The contingent then marched on board, the infantry and most of the artillery embarking on board the Iberia, which takes 600 of the men, the remaining 200, with the horses and stores, being conveyed by the Aus- tralasian. Enthusiastic cheers were given as the vessels steamed away. BRITISH MAILS ROBBED. Kowri, TUESDAY.—Khasim El Moos Pasha has arrived here from Metammeh with company of black troops. The native in charge of the mails from the British force at Gak- dul is reported to have been attacked on his way here by marauders, who robbed him of the mails and his camels, and nearly killed the man himself. MOVEMENTS OF THE MAHDI. VIENNA, WEDNESDAY NIGHT. The Mubashir learns from Dongala that the Mandi has given orders to break up the camp at Omdurman and proceed north towards Metam- meh. The Mandi, it adds, intends to make Metammeh and Shendy his chief centres of military operations for the junction of the roads to Khartoum. Communication is to be kept up by the steamers captured at Khartoum which Gordon turned into ironclads. A line of dahabeas will form a floating bridge between Shendy and Matammeh. CAIRO, THURSDAY MORNlNG.—According to reports from native sources which are believed to be reliable, the Mandi with a large force has left Khartoum, and is advancing northwards along the Nile. No confirmation of the report has yat reached the British authorities here. Among foreign residents at Cairo the prospect of war be- tween England and Russia has produced great excitement and much jubilation. REMOVAL OF HEADQUARTERS. KORTI, WEDNESDAY —The headquarters will shortly move to Dongola. The troops are to be quartered at various points along the Nile, and the steamers, nuggars, and whalers are being got ready fbr this movement, which is , rendered necessary by climatic reasons. The temperature 4 here ii now 104 degrees in the shade.

A supplementary estimate was issued on Thursday show- ' ing the amount that will be required to meet further de- ficiencies in the Army Estimates for the current year, caused by additional expenditure for ordinary services and for military operations in the Soudan. The net total of the amount required is £942,000, of which £672000 is due to the Soudan.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

I The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present Messra. Greening (chairman), Darbyshire, Caldwell, Apple- ton, Brown, Ratcliffe, Wm. Houghton, Blackhurst, Dr. Mackie, Harrison, Cooper, Jeans, Forster, Kilshall, and Roberts ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

div.head: COUNTY RATES.
div.p: THE COUNTY RATES.

In submitting the -cheques,' ilie--(SL-I#7lt. It said the total county rate was £2,177 16s ld against £1,6113 18s ad for the corresponding ball of last year, being an excess of £.560 17s HU He noticed there was an increase of £283 10s lid in the county rate proper ; an increase of £3lB Is Id under the. heading of county. lunatic asylums, and an

increase of £ll4 7s 81 because of the constabulary of the Warrington division, and there was also an increase of £2O 15s 4d under the heading of county prisons at Preston and Kirkdale. These were the increases, but on the other hand

there were a few small decreases.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said he was very much etarded at the increase. (Hear, hear.) He supposed the amount was collected under the new scale, and he had been in hopes that it would be less. It seemed to him that times were growing worse, yet more money was wanted. He should be glad if any means could be taken to lessen the increase in this respect. (Hear, bear.)—Dr. MACKIE said one good result of these increases would be to strengthen the hand of those gentlemen of both political parties, who were anxious to get some scheme of county government. It was evident to him that the expenditure in connection with lunacy was going to increase at an en- ormous extent—Mr. BLACKIIIIRSr moved, and Mr. HARM. SON seconded that the cheques be paid, and the proposal was adopted.

div.head: TRE GRANTING OF SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: TRE GRANTING OF SCHOOL FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported 0;i -titers bad been 95 Cases dealt with, 61 old and 34 new.—Mr. BLACKHURST, in moving tha adoption of the report, said he regretted that the number of these CASOS were increasing.:-Dr. MACKIE said he should wish to strongly recommend tnat if they as a Board could directly assist in reducing the number of cases brought before them, or if they could do it through opera- tion on the Town Council or the inhabitants of Warrington generally. He did not know anything more painful than to see 90 cases of respectable persons broueht up, none o/ whom were abs.dute paupers, and most of them mothers with young children. From a report which would be pre- sented to the Town Council be SAW that there had been no less than 330 cases brought before the magistrates, and that in a majority of cases tines were inflicted. It seemed to him that the expenditure on education like that on lunacy ought to be closely watched, and it wes a fact that they spent in Warrington something like £16,000 a year on education. It was a question whether these poor people who applied for the payment of their children's pee could not be treated in some other way. He did not know , whether or not it would be possible to get up some sympa- thetic and philanthropic movement, and get the Town Council and their fellow-townsmen to shore with them to get a school for these poor waifs. He did not 'know whether anything could be done legally to get up an indus- trial school for these children, as he understood that when they went to the best of the ordinary schools with Beard of Guardian warrants, they got the cold shoulder, and-k was somewhat natural that they should, for they were less cleanly and well clothed than the other children.—Mr. HARRISON could not see how Dr. Mackie's suggestion was to be carried out. The Toxteth Board of Guardians had, he believed, entered into some understanding with the Liverpool School Board by which they assented to the school attendance officer making inquiry, and the Guardians took as ,a matter of course what the officer staggested. That was done with a view to mitigate to some extent the annoy- ance which these poor felt at having:to go before a commit- tee, but still that course did not diminish the numbers, but would have rather an opposite tendency. The whole ques- tion was a social problem surrounded with difficulties and hardships.—Dr. MACKIE : And a novel one.—Mr. HARRISON said the cases were very frequent before magistrates in which the fees were paid, and still the parents did not send their children to school. They would be surprised to see .the facility with :which these people paid down the penalties of ss, although they seemed scarcely to have clothes enough to cover their nakedness.— Mr CALD WELL said it was often a case of semi-starvation with thcse poor children. (Hear, hear.) Many of them were sent to school with empty stomac'es, and they wanted clother and food as well as school fees. For himself he would be glad if something could las done, but at present he did not see they could adopt a better plan than they had. If they had a school board the rates would be increased and the children wonld be no better looked after than they were now, and perhaps not so well.—Mr. Aeet.strote could not see how anything more than they were doing could be done. —Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that there had been a good deal of imposition on the committee by people applying for fees who ought not to have applied. He was of opinion that when anyone wanted school fees allowed the least they could do was to come and apply for them -Mr. BLACKIIIIRST said the committee acted in the most humane way they could, and he did not see what further could be done as the law stood at present. There were, however, as Mr. Derby- shire said, many people who applied who ought not to do so. —Mr. JEANS thought that if Dr. Mackie's suggestion was carried out they would be liable to a good deal of imposi- tion. If it were possible to form a ragged school under the present law it might be a good thing, but there was no law to enable them to do so. The position Mr. Mundella took up was that if Corporations had not sufficient power they must get the power by setting up a school board, which meant a great expenditure to the town. He happened to live in Sankey where they had had a school board thrust upon them, the result being that even now before they had got the school built their school rates had leaped up from Is to is 61 in the —The CHAIRMAN said it had been very distressing indeed to have to investigate some of the cases that had been brought before them, but there were also cases in which it had been, attempted to impose upon them in the most flagrant manner. But if they were to start a separate school for these poor children each would still have to be investigated before being admitted.—The CLERK said be did not see why the committee should not fix a principle upon which school fees would be granted. It seemed to him that if they would agree that in certain circumstances where the income of a family per bead was limited to so small a sum that it was not reasonable to expect them to pay school fees these fees might be granted as a matter of course.—The minutes of the committee were then con- firmed, and the discussion dropped.
THE PENHETH VACCINATION STATION.

With regard to the removal of the above station, Mr. B. Hobson, vaccination officer, wrote as follows :—" Yours to hand referring to myself and Dr. Gornall selecting a suit- able piaci; for Penketh vaccination station. The Penketh Infant School cannot be obtained again for that purpose, as the same cause exists which obliged us to leave and seek another place; there is no possibility of that room being available for use as the vaccination station so as to agree with the original contract of Dr. Gornall, the public vacci- nator. The other changes made from time to time during a period extending nearly to 20 years, were made from force of circumstances, never thinking the changes were done con- trary to any existing law custom or duty to the Board. Bat as you say, the changes had never received the sanction of the Board or the approval of the Local Government Board. Trusting it is never' too late to mend,' it follows that we must commence de nem. Dr. Gornall and myself have jointly c -insidereel the matter and recommend the room at the Liberal Club as the most suitable place for the station. As for comfort, I think it will compare as favourably to the Conservative Club as one of the new third-class compart- ments of a railway carriage to one ef the old style of third- class, open from end to end would compare." (Laughter.) —The Grumman asked the Clerk to explain how the vaccination stations were chosen, by whom they were chosen, and by whose authority the choice was decided upon ?—The CLERIC: By the Board of Guardians, approved by the Local Government Board, and endorsed upon the contract of the vaccination officer. He found that the Pen- keth one was fixed at the Infant School, Penketh, and that there had been no change in respect of the station.—The CHAIRMAN said he thought the Clerk had made it quite plain that the only place sanctioned by the Board of Guar- dians for the vaccination station at Penketh was the In- fant School. It had been shifted from there because those who belonged to the school would not have them there to the Wesleyan School, from which they had also to shift. The station, after some other changes, was fixed at the Con- servative Club, and now it was proposed to shift it to the Liberal Club. It was for that Board to say which place should be endorsed on the contract. He thought that some- body—he did not know who it was—was to blame for not giving them notice of the removals, but he gathered that it was through ignorance that this bad not been done.—Mr CALDWELL said that Mr Hobson knew Penketh as well as anybody, and both he and Dr Gornall said the Liberal Club was the beet place —Mr,Damovsmax wanted to know who had been paying for the station since it was removed from the Infant Schoolroom.—The CLERIC: This Board.—Mr DABBISHIRE thought it would be an illegal payment, and I that those officers who had removed the station from place

.—........ _____ to place ought to have paid it out of their own pocket;. He should like to know how much they had paid to the Con- servative Club.—The CLERK said there had been no altera- tion in the payment. They had agreed to pay £2 a year, and that had been regularly paid. They must remember that the primary object was vaccination, and that vaccina- tion had been carried on most successfully in the Penketh district. (Hear, hear.)—Mr HARRISON said he had seen Dr Gornall himself since last meeting, and from what he had said he (the Mayor) thought that Mr Hobson had by no means given way to a flight of the imagination in describ- ing one place as very much superior to the other. It would appear to him therefore that they had only one course open to them.—Mr. FORSTER moved that the vac- cination station remain where it had been for the last three years, that was to say the Conservative Club. He main- tained that this place was suitable for the pur- pose of a vaccination station. He denied that I there was any political feeling in that matter, i although it had gone forth that there was. (Hear, I hear, and laughter.) He felt that the Board bad been treated 1 with very scant courtesy when an officer removed a station and then six or eight months after came to the Board and

aqied them to confirm what he had done. That was his , first objection. His second wee that ha did not think that, , he as a member of the Conservative Club at Penketb, should sit quietly there and hear it aspersed in the manner it had been, (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—ln answer to Mr. Jeans, Mr. FORSTER said the Conservative Clubroom was 40 feet by 15 feet and was very well lighted, ctn., while the Liberal Clubroom—although he had never bees in it—was only the front room of a cottage, and might be about 14 feet by 12, or 15 by 12. The Conservative Club, be thought, ought to be suitable enough as it had been used as a vaccination station for three years. Mr. CALDWELL : IS it quite as convenient as the so-called Liberal cottage. (Laughter.)—Mr. FonsTER: It i..—Mr. APPLETON seconded Mr. Forster's proposal.—Mr. BLACKHURST said that at last meeting Mr. Forster seemed to impute that there was political feeling in that matter. He wished to ask whether Mr. Hobson was Liberal or Tory. —The Crtataxesr : No, no.—Mr. FORSTER : I am not Mr. Hobson's conscience keeper.—The CHAIRMAN : That is quite sufficient —Dr. MACKIE thought that attentisn ought to be given to the wishes of the medical officer.—Mr. BLACKILURST 'Proposed that Mr. Hobson's recommendation be adopted —Mr. RATCLIFFE seconded.—Mr. Hartarsota and the CHAIRMAN also supported this proposal.—On being put to the vote there were nine voted for Mr. 131ackhurs1's pro- posaLand seven for Mr. Forster's, the former being conse- quently declared carried.—Mr. DARENs/ILRE : Are we pay- ing for two places, Mr. Chairman ?—The CHAIRMAN. I cannot tell you about that.—The CLERK stid all be had to pay was the 40s.—Mr. FORSTER : They are paying for two places.—The CLERK: That is their look out ; we shall only pay for one. THE COST OP VACCINATION CASE'S: NO.CRED/T GIVEN. Mr. Comm, the Earlestown and Newton vaccination officer, attended and state?. that the magistrates' clerk had refused to issue any more summonses withont pay, and that the clerks told him that distress 'warrants would net be made Out without seven shillings and sixpence for etch warrant. —ln answer to the Chairman, the CLERIC stated that the practice for many years had been on receipt of bille to pay them by cheque. The Board had reasonably objected to charges for work deemed unnecessary and for fees they thought in:excess of the fees allowed by the scale, and they bad directed him to make such objections, but leaving it afterwards to his discretion, he paid the bill. He supposed the clerks were displeased • to have their charges criticised, but the Board were justified in whit they did and he did not agree with the reasons for the demands although he paid. The construction put upon words seemed unten- able, and it was certainly contrary to the old practice. He perfectly well remembered the scale of fees when adopted in 1847, and in that scale similar words were used and no per- son had se much to do with the practice of the neighbour- ing magistrates courts, county or borough, or with the regulation of the fees charged as he had down to the begin- ning of the year 1862, and what he now held to be right was what was universally thought right in all those years. With regard to the demand to be peid beforehand, it might be an advantage to know that work was not to be done until paid for. Fees were charged for work unasked for and of no U 5 . If done it WAS an unnecessary and useless thing to do, so if the magistrates' clerks' would refuse to do work until paid, in that respect advantage would result. (Hear, hear.) —Mr. P. CALDWELL theught it was rather high-handed con- duct on the part of Mr. Buckton, and that he was not treat- ing them with courtesy.—Mr. JEANS thought the best way was to pay beforehand. The clerks might refuse to prepare what was necessary until paid.—lt was decided that the Vaccination Officer should ascertain the fees demanded for summonses and warrant:, and apply at the clerk's office for the amount. This was all the business of interest.
WARRINGTON BIND OF How UNION: CHI L DREN's FES TIVAL.

The second Children's Festival promoted by this union was held on Monday evening in the Public Hall, when there was a good attendance.—The chair was occupied by the Rev. JOHN YONGE, who, in addressing the meeting, said they must all feel a deep interest in the Bind of Hope movement, for one reason—if not for !limy 'Lore—that it began at the right end. It went upon the admirable prin- ciple that preveution was better than cure. All know how difficult it was, sometimes how almost hopeless it seemed to be, to rescue those who had become victims of the vice of intemperance. Old teetotallers would know how terribly difficult it was to rescue men and women who, from the habits, perhaps, ef long years, had become the complete slaves of this over-mastering vice. The Band of Hope movement set itself easier work to do. It sought to train up boys and girls to total abstinence from childhood. If they trained their children in boyhood and girlhood to the habit of sobriety, and of having nothing whatever to do with alcoholic drinks, they might hope they would con- tinue in their maturer years to practise that same abstin- ence, and so be saved from the many temptations with which drinking was surrounded. He bad occasionally viewed with feelings almost of horror the habits which some parents had, even in these enlightened days, of giv- ing their children drinks of the description to which he had referred. He hoped that the feeling of the meeting was unanimously against such a parental practise as that. If there were any present who were in the habit of encourag- ing their children to take such drinks, let him in passing say that it was a matter that should engage their serious censideration, whether they were not exposing their chil- dren to a danger that micht pro've disastrous to them in the not far distant future. Recently, under the auspices of the Warrington Band of Hope Union, there had been an ex- amination held of a number of young people who had, first of all, been trained in certain of the principles of total ab- stinence, and certain physical aspects of it. A competitive examination had been held and a number of candidates were expecting to receive priz.ts bye-and-bye. That experiment had been successful as far as it had gone, and he hoped that the movement would now be taken up more heartily by all the schools in the union, in order that more young people might be trained to intelligent thought and real practical knowledge on this important matter. He the other day read with feelings of gratification remarks made from the Bench by Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, to the effect that he was glad to be able to state from recent statis- tics of crime that, compared with a certain period—he thought it was ten years back—there was considerably less crime in the country to-day than at the previous period men- tioned. Considering that the population had greatly in- creased, it was a great gratific ttion to know that mime had diminished, and also to know that the learned judge de- clared it as his opinion that one of the prime factors in producing this result was the 'About. of temperance advo- cates. (Applause.) They must go forwatd with the hope that the day was coming when their country should be de• livered from a stigma which rested upon it at present of being, perhaps, the most drunken nation in the world. Might the time quickly come when temperance and sobriety should win those glorious victories which were due to the cause. (Applause.)—Subsequently Mr. F. Sykes, a tem- perance advocate, addressed the meeting.—During the even- ing a miscellaneous programme was ably rendered by the members of the choir, assisted by Miss L Horton and Mr W H Wallington. Mr C H Pigot was conductor and Mr F Booth accompanist. Both Miss Horton and Mr Walling-

ton were applauded for their songs, and they, in conjunction with all who had contributed to the success of the festival, were heartily thanked, a vote of thanks to the chairman bringing the meeting to a close.

TRESPASSING IN PI7E-SrIT 0-1:6-A-ME.—Thomas Wright, a kbourer, living at Widnes, was summoned at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesdiy for trespassing in pursuit of game, on land at Crouton on the 16th February, over ' which Colonel Parkes possesses the rignt of shooting. The defendant did not appear, and as he had been previously convicted for a similar offence, he was fined 40s. and costs.

DR. O'HARA CHARGED WITA FORGING COUNTY COURT Sunstonsos.—On Saturday, Dr. O'Hara, of Prescot, was brought up on remand, before Mr W L Evans,-on a charge Of issuing forged processes of the Si. Helens County Court. It appeared that Mrs Ellen Fairhurst, of the Shamrock beerheuse, Tea-street, Prescot, owed the prisoner a sum of money, and he served upon her a paper which he purported to be a summons from the St. Helens County Court. On the application of Superintendent Barker the prisoner was again remanqd for a week, the Bench refusing to grant bail. PRYSCOT GUREDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting of th'S Board was held on Thursday, Mr Hall in the chair. A lett r was read from the Local Government Board acknowledgirg the receipt of plans for providing, infirmary accommodation at the Workhouse, and promising to examine them as soon as possible. The Clerk submitted correspondence he had had with the clerk to the Widnes School Board on the sub. ject of providing accommodation for deaf and dumb and blind children in Widnes. A letter was read from Mr Rock, accountant, of Widnes, in which it was stated that the Local Government Board, in reply to his inquiry, had suggested that he should apply to the Guardians for per- mission to take a copy of the reasons of the district auditor for allowing certain sums charged in the accounts for 1854 to which he objected.—The Chairman moved that the books, having been audited and closed, should not be re-opened. Los, oF FISHING BOATS AND 18 LIVES.-- Int( D. n'twas received in Glasgow on Thursday thAt three fishing boats were lost off the coast of Lewes on Wed- night, with 18 men. A large fleet of boats left and other ports in the island early in the days nsetosdroloYway and Proceeded to the cod and ling fishing ground, about 15 miles out. The wind was blowing violently from the north-east, and a sudden change to the south-west caused a heavy sea to set in along the Ness and Broad Bay coasts. The boats at once made for the nearest harbours, and about three o'clock the Ness Beet arrived off the port of that name. Two of the boats, each containing a crew of six men, were, however, lost while being beached, and those on board perished. A third boat was lost in Broad Bay, and six of the crew of eight men were drowned. Two were picked up clinging to oars by the crew of another boat. Orrtar.o.LursgEr. If, as the Tories urge, the country is disgusted with the failure of the Government expedition to relieve General GORDON, they will fall in with any arrangement which enables them to take advantage of any feeling there may be on this subject before it has wholly died away. An election upon the old franchise, and by the old constituencies, would, taking all things into account, be regarded by the nation as a fraud, and would be followed by another election as soon as the Franchise Bill and the Seats Bill were in force. The Tories have nothing therefore to hope from such a Parliamentary " fluke" as would turn the Government out of office before the pass- ing of the Seats Bill. They could not retain office for a month in the present Parliament, not even if they took two of their recent con- verts—Mr. FoRsTER and Mr. PARNELL—inIo a brand new Cabinet; and we are quite sure they have no desire to prejudice their case by an appeal to the people until the people as a whole an be appealed to. It thus hap- pens that the failure of the Opposition to defeat the Government is alike good for the Opposition, for the Government, and for the Nation.

EARLESTOWN has for some time back been growing more a,nd more famous for football; but the winning of the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup is a feather in the hat of the local team of which they may justly feel very proud. A cursory glance at the situation would suggest that the Odds were a long way against a team formed in a.small town hold_ ing its own against the teams of picked players which can be found in such a com- munity as Liverpool, with its 600,000 inhabi- tants. But facts dispose of speculation, and the facts are that the " Earlestown lads " have from the first shawn an aptitude for football ; that they "all but " won the Cup last year, and that on Saturday last they suc- ceeded in carrying off the much-coveted trophy. The victory was highly gratifying to the inhabitants, and when the team' reached home the various members of it were treated as so many conquer- ing heroes. SHAKESPERE tells us that when CLEOPATRA sailed down the Cyndus "the city cast its people out upon her." It was pretty much the same at Earlestown, for though it is not a city, it has its people, and they were quite as enthusiastic in their way as the citizens who rent the air in welcome of , the beautiful Queen of Egypt. It was felt I not only that the Eatlestown team had won, i but that they hwl `.v,".1 Last year; they carried all before than Until the final I contest, when, ?.frer a. well-played goat% they were beat'.:.n by Everton by one goal to none. As 't runner-up" on that occasion, they were entitled to and obtained silver medals. This year they have again had to encounter Ever- ti in the final—a circumstance which speaks volumes for the merits of both teams—and skill and fortune have this time favoured them, for they have beaten Everton as Ever- I ton beat them—by one goal to none. The ; two teams are obviously well matched, or there would have been more than two goals to record in two great contests ; but Earlestown, as the last winners, must now be garded as the premier team. Some bad feel- ing has been shown by the respective sup- porters of the two teams; and, as this is the worst element in these contests, it is to be hoped that the officials of the various clubs will exert themselves as much as possible to reduce it to a minimum. Let us by all means have local patriotism.; it is a healthy stimulant, so long as love of "our noble selves" does not degenerate into hatred of others. But this is the time for rejoicing rather than for lecturing, and We heartily congratulate the Earlcstown football team upon, having won "a famous victory."

TnE Lymm Local Board is under tireat of being boycotted," and yet, judging from the repoet of the proceedings at the monthly meeting on Thursday, the members are by no •meens miserable. They seem, if any- thing, to be rather more lively then usual. The particular offence which has 'brought impending (loom over their heads consists in supplying this journal, in its turn, with a legal advertisement. Our contemporary, the " Warrington Guardian," as one of the members of the Board remarks, -seems to "want everything," and because, in this ,instance, it has not had what it was not entitled to ihave, the Board Is telbe " boy- .cotted proceedings for the future are not to be -reported in that journal. This must be .teTrible, especially, as the Chair- man observes, to those who ."-make long speeches" It is, perhaps, fortunate that the " Guardian " is not the only newspaper cir- culating in this part of the country, and the Local Board may after all survive. It is just possible that the inhabitants of Lymm have hitherto lived in the delusion that our contemporary reported the proceedings of the Board in their interests. They will now know that it does not take them into ac- count, e=ept as ratepayers who find the money for advertisements. The Editor of the " Guardian " will of ,course be as good as his word in doing what he threatens, and —"we shall see what we shall see." The condition of the poor "Ija.c.kdaw of Rheims," whose feathers, under the car- dinal's curse, "turned all the wrong way," w:11 be happiness .itself com- pared with that of the members and officials of the Lymm Local Board when " boycotted " by the " Guardian." They have our sympathy; it is with fear and , trembling on their behalf that -we await I the result.

CONGREGLTIONAL UNION,—The Lancashire Congrega- tional Union vet on Wednesday in the Albion-street Chapel, Ashton-under-Lyne. After the delivery by the President the Rev. R. Bast (Bolton), of his inaugural address, various subjects were discussed, includiug a resolution urging upon her Majesty's Gevernment that "in the interests of righteousness and peace the war in the Soudan should be brought to an end as speedily as possible," and expressing also the opinion that "no party in the State is so well qualified as that now in power, headed by Mr. Gladstone, to bring -about that hap• pv result." This reslution moved by Mr. E. Dawson (Lancaster), and seconded by tbo Rev. S. Pearson (Liver- pool) was passed usanimously.

LIBERAL CANDIDATES FOR SOUTH-EAST LANCASHIRE.—A correspondent says :—" The chairman of the National Re- form Union Executive Committee (Mr R Barlow) stated at a meeting of representatives of Liberals of the Heywood division, held a few days ago, that he had the following in- formation on good authority, viz., that the Middleton divi- sion would be contested by Colonel Schwabe, Prestwich by Mr A B Rowley, Gorton by Mr R Peacock, Westhoughton by Mr Edward Cross, and Stretford by Mr D Adamson." It appears he was upon a scaffolding superintending the erection of chemical plant, when the structure gave way, and he with several other gentlemen was precipitated to the ground, a distance of 30 feet. He was unconscious for five days, but it is satisfactory to learn that be is now pro- gressing favourably. Mr R H Davies, of the firm of Messrs Golding, Davies, and Co, Widnes, Was With Mr Hargreaves at the time of the accident. The injured gen- tleman's wife and brother, Mr James Hargreaves, F.J.C. and F.C.S.. have since departed for France to attend to his requirements. FIRE AT WIDNES DOM....About four o'clock on Sunday morning P.C. Holbrook discovered that a shed covering a moveable steam crane on the quay side at West Bank Dock was burning fiercely. Ile at once gave an alarm, and P.S. Clarkson and eeeeral constables were quickly on the spot, but the dimes bed obtained such a hold upon tl.e structure that it was considered useless to attempt to extinguish them, and the order for the ere engine was countermanded. The crane has sustained little injury, but the shed, which had only been standing about a week, was totally destroyed. Fifteen pounds will cover the damage, which is not insured. How the fire originated is a Mystery, as John Jones, of Irwellestreet, the engine driver, asserts he raked out the fire on Seturday night. XTTEMPrED SUICIDE AT RUNCJEN.—Mrs Leah Carter, wife of George Carter. of 25, Surrey-etreet, Runcorn, attempted to c immit suicide on Tuesday afternoon. About five o'clock her little daughter returned from echool and found her mother lyitig on the bedroom floor, blood flowing from a wound in the throat, which had eyideatly been in- flicted by a razor. The girl at once ran to the house of her grandfather, Mr William Stanway, grocer, Lewlanels-read, and informed him of her mother's condition. The wound is not a dangerous one, and under the care of Dr Mac- Dougall she is proeresseng favourably. No reason can be assigned for the rash act, but about 3 weeks age Mrs Carter fell down the stairs and injured her head, and it is con- jectured that the injeries have led to sligkt mental de- rangement. ODADBTONE AND DlSEXcariZENT.—Noticing the answer which Mr. Gladstone has given to the question," Are the bishops and clergy of the Cnurch of En4land State- paid?" the ki6erator says :—" Therr,uestion was really an- swered once for all by what Parliament did in 1869. In that year the Legislature passed the Act for putting an end ts the Establishment of the Church inlzeland; and the answer to .the question was given by theltct that in disestablich• ing the Church it also disendowed it. Half a million of money was giverr to the Irish Church by Parliament inffieu of recent endowments, and the bishers and clergy and other officers of the Church were compensated for their life in- terests. But,with those exceptions the property by which tho Church had previously been enskyorted was taken away from it, and since then that property has been applied to secular purpous for the beneEt of te whole Irish people. "Chat was the reply which Parliament gave to the quetics in 3,869; and it -ic exactly the sort of reply 'which Parliament will give again when the Chtercheolv England and Wales and Scotland came to be disestablished."

A FEROCIOUS DOG AT Wssrote.—On Monday at Run- corn Felice Court, Phee")e Barrow, landlady of the Royal Oak Inn, Wes'on, was summoned for disobeying an order of the magistrates directing her to keep a dangerous dog under proper control.—P.C. Cooper deposed that he served an order upon the defendant on the 20. h November. On the 20th February he saw the dog mentioned in the order run- ning about the streets of the village. He had also seen it at large previously.—The defendant said the dog was " a little playful soft thing," and was kept chained up hdlf its time. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, WIDNES A mutual improvement society has just been formed in cm n ction with the Lacey-street Wesleyan Sunday schools. The inaugural meeting was held in Lacey-street sclool on Monday evening, when about 100 Persons sat down to supper. Short appropriate addresses were delivered by the president, the vice-presidents, and Mr T S Swale. _ . _

SCALDED TO DEATH AT RUNCORN.—John Cross, 28 veers of age, of Surrey-street, Runcorn, wh ) was employed as a labourer at Messrs Hazlehurst's Soap Works, died on Thurs- day night from injuries received on the 17th ult. In some manner, at present unexplained, the deceased fell int) a well containing boiling lees, and his agonising cries brought to his assistance a youth named Booth, who aided him to escape from his Unfortunate position. He was terribly scalded about the lower parts of the b .o*, and although Dr. McDougall has been in constant attendance he succumed to his injuries as sated. DROWSED WHILST Dula AT WIDNES —Eistt Hunting- , don, young man, who lived at Egreinont, and Was employed as fireman on board the ousting steamer Phoebe Gertrude, was drowned in the W,dnes West Bank Dock on Wednes- day m Huntingdon was drinking heavily in the town on Tuesday night, and it is supposed that when re- turning to his vessel he lit his way and fell in"o the water. About two o'clock a person sleeping on heard A vessel heard i cries of distress, bat upon getting up was enable to see any- thing. The water in the dock was subseqlently run off, and 1 the dead body of Huntingdon was found at the bottom.— Yesterday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inqiest at the Commercial Inn on the body of the deceased. After bearing the evidence, which bore out the above narrative, a verdict of " accidental death" was re- I corded. Several of the jurymen expressed the opinion that some of the bridges across the various parts of the docks ; were too narrow and in a dangerous state.—Mr. Forrand, who represented the London and Nerth-Western Railway Company, said he would communicate with tha company's engineer on the subject. THE SHIP CANAL; AND THE Gas BILL—The Farlia- . .

mentary and Legal Committee had resolved that the follow- ing addition be made to No. 5 of the Commissioners' pro- tecting clauses for insertion in the Ship Canal Bill :—" And the company shall provide, free of charge, the necessary motive power for towing all vessels laden with cargoes for or from the Runcorn Docks along the said canal between Eastham and Runcorn." It was also resolved that 33 letter should be sent to Messrs Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., enclos- ing draft of clauses the Board thought might form a basis of arrangement, but the same were submitted without e.re. judice ; and stating that should the promoters desire an in- terview, the Committee would ba glad to meet a deputa'ion at Runcorn on such convenient day as they might fix. It was also revolved that the following report of the Runcora Gas Bill Commiteee be adopted :—" We beg to report that a meetieg of the ratepayers having been held on Thursday, the sth day of February, to pass a resolutlen authorising the Committee to oppose in Parliament a private bill now before Par. ilament, entitled "A Bill to enable the Runcorn Gasp Cotnpany to raise additional capital to coastruat new worka I and for other purposes" with a view to obtain the Meer- tion of clauses embodying tha following provisions :—(1) to reduce the standard price of gas; (2) that the di vidende undermo circumstanc:s be more than 10 pr cent, on the Capital raison under the Act of 1847, 7 per cent. on the c 'pita( raised under the proposed Act, and 5 per cent, upon preference shares ; (3) that the sliding scale (section 13) be omitted from the Bill so fa- as it affects the increase of standard dividends; (4) that the prescribed illuminating power of the gas to be fixed at 18 candles; (5) that the maximum price of gas be 3321 p-r 1 003 cubic feet subject to 2d per 1,000 cubic feet discount; (8) that any balance of profit after p tying the standard votes of dividends be applied to the reduction of the price of gas to consumers; (7) that the Commissioners may from time to time be allowed to ap- point a person to an lit the accounts of the Gas Company in the interests of the consumers. Such meeting of rate- payers having decided against the adoptiot. of the resolutim, this committee think it well to intimate that they consider their functions have terminated."— Mr Lightburn, in moving the confirmation of the minutes and the adoption of the report, said hie individual opinion was that both the gts and water works ought lo ha the pro- perty of the town, and that Runcorn wool I nevzr again have a better opportunity of purchasing the interes a of the Gas Company than at present.—Mr Speakman seconded the motion, and endorsed the sentiments of Mr Lightburn. —The Chairman said he thought the time was a good one to purchase before the ratepayers' meeting. It was a very different question that day. Be believed the vote at that meeting increased the value of the concern by some the u• settle of pounds. It scored not be wise for the Board to exertain any idea of purchasing the gas works, because 'there was no possibility of receiving from the concert: any- thing like eufficimt to p.y the interest on the La,mey they would have to get. he minutes were adopted. _ The monthly meeting WaA held at the offices, Bridgewater.- street, on Wednesday. Mr. J. Pritcbar.: ;presided, and there were present Messrs R. Lea, T. Norman, P. Briscoe, and F. Rigby (clerk). Tilt NEW t-,CHOOLS —Messrs Norman, Lea, and Briscoe were appointed a Building Committee during the construc- tion of the new Board sctiool —A cheque of £5O was passed. for payment to Messrs F. and G. Holmes for services in connection with the drawing of plans.

. -- THE REV. W. Pansrow AND TIIE BOARD.— The Clerk read the copy of a letter written to the Rev. William Pres- ton applying for the payment of rent due, and stating that it would be necessary that the tenancy of the school should. cease unless Mr. Preston gave the Bo rd an undertaking that each gnat terly payment shoalcl be punctually made The following letter was received in repl.v :—.• Trinity Par- sonage.—Gentlemen,—l am erievei that you should be so distressed at the nonreceipt of your reut, but the fault has .been due not to laity but to the fact of an empty ex- chequer, which has to be replenished by my youag men and myself picking up a shilling where Nve can. I hope for the future it will be fuller and SO better aide to meet demands. I beg to enclose cheque for amount due, aril I remain, yours ;aithf ally, WM. PRESTON."—Mr. Norman : That is satisfactory.—Mr. Briscoe : I:5 a very uncertain way of getting money.—The Chairman : It was net on these conditions quite that we 1.. t the school, was it?— Mr. BriscJe : No.

THE EDECATION DEPARTMENT ON THE SCHOOL DIFFI- CULTY.— the Clerk read the following letter which he had forwarced by the direction of the Beird to the Education D.ipertment :—" I am directed by my Board to acknowledge receipt of your letters of the 23-d and Nth January, enclose. jog copies of letters from Canon Barclay, Mr. Sampson, and Mr. Rogerson, respecting the non-atter dance at school of the boy Wright. In view of the conflicriug statements therein contained my Board desire me to state that they have found it impossible to arrive at a sat- isfactory conclusion in the case, more especially as they are of opinion that they have indisputable evidence to prove that not only t? boy Wright but ot er children have been refused admission at the three schools in question when they were by no means full. lam to remind you that ia my previous leter I pointed ,alt that Wright's, far from being an isolated case, is typical ee a pre-eiee which for some months has obtained in Runcorn and frus- trated the Board in their efforts -to ceues the children of poor parents to be educated. In these circumstances my Board humbly submit that an exhaustive investigation is warranted, and they have therefore directed me to suggest that it wield be expedient for my Lords te iestruct HAL Inspector to make such inquiries upon the spot as he ally deem sufficient to determine the true coneition of affairs. As an example of another difficelty my Board hare to con- tend agaicst, I have been directed to enclose to you a cut- ting from a local newspaper reporting the c IS2 eta Runcorn School Board prosecution, where the master of the Wesleyan Boys' ecnool admitted on oath that school fees tendered in respect of the then current week bad been applied to the payment of fees owing in respect of a previous reek, and that the bay was refused admission into school and sent home for more inenev." "Education Department, 3:d March, ISSs.—Sir,—Adverting to your letter of the sth ultimo, lain now to state that it has been considered in con- nection with your earlier letter of the Bth Jermery, and with the letters (copies of which you already possess) I written to this Department by the Rev. Canon Barclay, Mr. W. H. Rogerson, and Mr. John Simpson. It appears therefrom that the (lifficulties experiencedlby your Board in securing the school attendance of Joseph Wright, and of other children in similar circumstances, are in the opinion lof the Board seriously increased by the prac- tice adopted in Holy Trinity school of raising the ordinary fee to 61 a week as a punishment for gross irregularity. My Lords have reqaested Mr. Rogerson as Use correspondent for the Trinity School to in- vite his managers to rescind the resolution under which this practice is enforced, so that one of the obstacles wYch the Board have encountered ire the discharge of their statutory duty may be removed. I may point oat that a scheme has beeu succesefully worked in several voluntary schools of raising the general fee by some very small amount and then of returning the extra sum to regular echolars. The ques- tion whether this scheme can be usefully adopted in Rune corn shculd he carefully censidercd by the managers at National, Holy Trinity, and Wesleyan echeols. My Lees, hope that the managers will also endeavour to make eacb. general arrangements as will secure more harmony aniceg the different echools. and aleo more efficient co-operation with the School Board of which body the managers in sereral instances appear to ba themselves members.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, G. MILLEIi."-- , Mr. Lea : Humph.—The Chairman It carries out our j view in a great measure.—The Clerk said the suggestion of vie department worked with many voluntary s.ebeets ire this way; if the children attended rnAlelerlY, the small extra fee was returned to them as a bonus.—'Mr. Lea said they , distributed prizes at Holy. Trinlty--Tbe Clerk :But ' money. He added that it was, however, a matter of internal policy for the schools.—Mr. Norman : It is a great pity Ithat the schools cannot work harmoaionsly together.—The 1 Clerk : This letter removes the obstacle we have had ta fight against.—The Chairman : Se it does.

div.head: ADJOURNED MEETING. THE VACANT SEATS.
div.p: THE ADJOURNED MEETING. THE VACANT SEATS.

The adjourned meeting was held on Thursday eveniug, when Mr Shaw presided, and there were present—Messrs Norman, Dobson. Harris, Williams, Whittaker, White, Bris- coy, Lake, Lightbarn Fisher, Taylor, Speakman, IV H Lin- ker (law clerk), W Brookes (secretary), and M Barker (sur- veyor). The object of the meeting WAS to fill op the loan• ces caused by the non-attendance of Mr IV Handley and the removal of Mr F Fairhurst to Preston,

Speakman said he hid res. pie:tante in proposing that Mc Henry Gila, saddler, Bridge-street, be appointed in place of Mr Fairhurst. Mr Grine was an old resident, highly respectable, and would make a very good Commis- sioner.—Mr Taylor seconded the motion.—Mr Lake begged to move an amendment. He had nothing against Mr Grine. He knew him t be a thoroug.hly honourable, upright busi- ness tnan, who would no doubt make a very efficient member of the Board. But in filling up the vacancy caused by Mr Fairhurst's retirement, they must remember that Mr Fair- hurst was elected at a contested election, and in opposition to the party represented by Mr Gtice, and to represent to a large extent the shop keeping element in the town. It was therefore desirable that they should appoint someone in his place who would occupy a similar position in regard to the ratepayers. Another thing was this : Mr Grice had been before the ratepayers and was not elected, and it seemed to him going in the teeth of the ratepayers to appoint him , now. He proposed as an amendment that Mr W H Boger- ; son, draper, of Bridge-street, be the me.nber in place of Mr Fairhurst. He would represent the same class of rate- payers as Mr Fairhurst did; he had a great deal to do with Mr Fairhurst's election, and he felt certain that his appoint- ment would meet with ttre approval of the ratepayers.—Mr Fisher seconded the amendment. He urged that if they elected Mr Roaerson they would never have cease to regret their action. He would fill the position of Commissioner usefully and honoursMy, and would be a credit not only to himself, but to the Board.—The Cuairman observed that in , that room they knew no party, each member discharged his ; duty with the ntfect of forwarding the well-being of the 'town, anal it rested with the membersto make a selection e the gentlemen preposed.—For Mr Rogerson there only voted I the mover and seconder ; and eigiit against. Mr Grine was I declared elected.

It was then seggested that it Rogerson should Ell Mr Handley's position, but Mr Lake said he should net advise hire to accept it, as be contended that the Botrd could not Make the appointment. After an interval Mr Rogerson was !appointed OE the motion of Mr Norman, seconded by Mr Williams. Mx Like voted against the motion.

div.head: ALLEGED ENIDELELEMENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED ENIDELELEMENT AT WIDNES.

1 At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr , W L Evans and Mr J Brock, William Hunt, a middle-aged man, woe brought up on remand charged -with having ob- tained by false pretences with intent to defraud various sums ,of money amounting to £3 19s lid from his employers, Messrs-Gaskell, Deacon, and Company.—Mr IV T Husband prosecuted, and Mr J W Knowles defended.—Mr Knowles Isaid with the Bench's permission the prisoner would restore ' the money to Messrs Oaskell, Deacon, and Cmpany, and I also make a donation to some charitable institution. If their worships decided to try the ease there he would ad- , vise his client to plead guilty and express his sorrow.—Mr Husband said the firm declined to take the money. They Iconsidered it a duty they owed to the public to prosecute. 1 insep! Morrison, manager of Messrs Gaskell, Deacon and !Company's works, Widnes, and residing at Farnvrorth, Wid- Inesovaid Wm. Hunt was formerly employed at Messrs Gas- kelt, 'Deacon and Company's. It was the prisoner's duty to enter the men's names and their wages in the bock celled tbe4' Foreman's time book," with regard to the work these 1 menhad done in:the yard. On March 12th the nameof Patrick Kilganuon was entered. For that week Kilgannon had not worked in the works, and consequently no wages wore due ' to him, but his name appeared in the wages sheet for £2e 43 4d4 and it ought not to have appeared. The writing was that of the wages clerk, who would get the particulars from the prisoner. Hunt had no business to receive wages. On April 2nd the name of John Kilmartin which appeared in the :pay sheet, but not in the time book, to the amount of 12s Sd. He had no recollection of such a man working for them. On April I.6th the name of James Tobin appeared lon the pay sheet, but he had not done anything that week. The amount of the entry was us 31. The prismer had no right to give those entries to the pay clerk. If the prisoner drew those items he had no right to do so. When these irregularities were discovered he brought the prieoner before him in his private office. on Friday, April 25tb, and I said names were appearing .in the pay sheets which were not in the foreman's book. The prisoner said they ought to have been omitted. Ho summoned one of the men, James Tobin. in his presence, and asked kine if he had reeeived the lie 31 which had been booked the week previously, namely, ou April IGth. Tobin strongly denied it. The prisoner said that he had given it to him. Kilgaunon, they happened to knew, was working at a neighbouring worka, and they seat for him. He came and said he had not received anything. The prisoner was suspended,— Cross-examined The primer had made no false coconuts. He had known the prisoner and his family all his life, and previous to this he considered the prisoner a thoroughly 1 respectable man, and be came to him with a very good ! !character. The firm did not wish to press the case, as,l ' it had been the means of breaking up his parents' home, 1 and his mother was dangerously ill in consequence. Henry Clarke, wages' clerk for Messrs Gasket!, Deacon.' land Co, and living at Peel House-lane, said be was wages' 1 clerk when the prisoner was employed at the works. frl looking over the took he found twelve eases altogether 'amounting to Vi 19s I.ld, the whole of which amount bad not been earned. Hunt applied to him and gets ticket from him in each case. except Tobin's. That would enable the prisoner to get the money from the cashier. Patrick Kilgalan, chemical labourer, said previous to the 2ad March, 1884, he was in the employ of Messrs Gaskell, Deacon, and Company. Re left their employ on that date.

Miscamr.Aiszons.:—Tbe following cases 0 drunkenness were dealt with :—Michael Griffin, in Bridge-street on Sat- urday, 43rd appearancs, dismissed ; John Mullins, in Ba'termarket-street, on Saturday night, fined ss, including ,costs; Mary Ann Pearson, in Brewn-street, fined 5s and costs; Annie Daffy, in Winwick-street, on Saturday, fined 5s and coats; Sarah Burns, in Winwick-street, on Satur- day, fined 103 and costs; Elizabeth Gorton, in B attermarket• street, on Satutday, dismissed • John Lawton, in Flag-lane, on the 22nd lined 5s and costs; Martin Burks and Ellen Connor, at Town Hill, fined 10s and costs cacti; Eliza- beth Rushton, ili Winwick-street, fined 55, including costs; Eliza Smith, in Bewserstreet, fined 103 and costs.—Har- riet Stringer and Patrick McCormick were fined Is each for allowing the chimneys of their houses to be on fire.—Tkos. Witness refused, and defendant pulled her out of the house by the hair, and hit her on- the ear.—Deftladant was bound over to keep the peace for six months.--Mary Ann Craden was summoned by Alice McKenny tot threaten- ing her on Friday last, at Orford.—Complainant stated that the defendant ran at her with a knife, and threatened her. After defendant received the summons she came to com- plaisant and knocked her to the floor.—Bound over to keep the peace for six months.—Alexander Catterall, Collins Green, was summoned by John Rothwell, also of Collins Green, for assaulting him on the 14th ult.—Mr Moore re- presented the defendant.—Complainant stated that on the day mentioned he was in the Pear lree Inn, Collins Green He asked the defendant's friend to pay for a drink for him when defendant knceked him down, and kicked him several times on the head.—Mr Moore called several witnesses, who proved that Rothwell was to blame, and the case was -dismissed.

In the Civil Service Estimates there appears an item of £B,OOO for repairing the damage done in the House of Commons and Westminster Hall by the dynamite ex- i plosions. LORD WOLSELEY'S EYESIGHT it said to be suffering from the climate of the Soudan. The noble lord has only the com- plete use of one eye at present, and if the other is seriously affected he would probably have to return home. At the Birmingham Assizes, on Wednesday, Win. Arthur Chandler, wholesale jeweller and diamond merchant, was sentenced by Mr. Justice Field to three months' imprison- ment without hard labour for fraudulent bankruptcy. SHOOTING A SWEETHEART.—ThOMSN Brooks, who resided at a viilege near Northampton, attempted to murder his sweethetrt, Mary 'rite, on Tuesday, by shooting her in the head with a revolver. He then tried te shoot his father and the housekeeper, and afterwards shot himself twice. He and Tile are in a dangerous condition. DYNAMITE OUTRAGE, IN IRELAND. The Protestant Church of Glenfin, in the parish of Kilteevock, county Donegal, was damaged by an explosion of dynamite on Tuesday. Two cartridges were exploded, carrying away two square feet of solid masonry. Other cartridges were found is the vicinity of the edifice. The district is descri- bed as very quiet, and the outrage has occasioned much sur- prise and indignation. ELvcriote NEWS: 'lwo NOMINATIONS—The Mid-Som- erset nomination took place at Wells. Mr. J. Kenelm Digby, of Sherborne Castle (Conservative), was the only candidate put forward, and consequently he was declared duly elected. There is no change in the representation. The West Gloucester nomination took place at the Town Hall, BllroleY, on Tuesday. Mr. B. St. John Aekers, Prinknash Park, Gloucestershire (Conservative), and Sir William Marling, Stanley House, Stroud, Gloucestershire (Liberal), were nominated. The polling will take place next Tuesday. At a Conservative meeting at Sleaford, Linco:nehire, on Tuesday night, Mr. Henry Chaplin con- sented to contest the division at the next electiore SINGULAR COTTON TRADE DISPPTE AT BOLTON.—The dispute at the mills of the Mill Hill Spinning Co., Bolton, has terminated. The company made deductions from the wages of some of their spinners as compensation for a num- ber of broken windows, but the men protested, and on the company refusing to return the sums deducted proceedings were commenced in the county court for their recovery. On Saturday week the company stopped all the men who had protested, and as a consequence the Operatives' Asso- ciation on the Monday brought out the spinners at both mlll3, 300 hands being thus thrown idle. It has since been agreed that the whole of the fines for broken windows which their been deducted should be returned, the men agreeing on part to endeavour to ascertain the cases where the windows had been broken wilfully or through careless con- duct, and in such eases the parties would have to pay the amount of the damage.
