visibly ixcreased, and there were cries for the cup-holders Ito "play up," and "sheet?' Every movement of the ball was watched with the keenest possible interest, and both teams were continually cheered. For a few momenta Ever- ton had the advantage, but the brotilere Green, who had been playing a spler.did back game, relieved the pressure, and Duxbucy and Renter, who had also been doing well, here showed some fine play. Play then became very ex- citing, and the Evertonians were hard pressed, Rich on the right and Ogden on the left indulging in some fine passing. A scrimmage at the Everton goal toek place, and the spec- tators expected to see Earleetovvn add another point, but the backs got the ball away, and Preston cleared the line amid the cheers of' their supporters. Bowter, Ogden, Rich, and Daenall showed some more seientific passing; but Finlay, playing in fine style, returned the ball to Richards, who in turn sent it to Itt‘Gill'S shot at goal again failed, and after the kick off Finlay returned with such judgment that Appleton, in saving, gave Everton a. inner, but again nothing came-ef it. The ball was now taken along by the Earlestown forwards, and Marriott missing his kick gave Simms and Dognall a splendid opportunity, but lindsay fisted the ball out. From a feel Simms centred to Dagnall, who.attemptedto•head the ball through, but Lindsay saved, and the baths relieved the pressure, though for a while ,EaLestown had the best of the play. In the last minute of p:ay, after some good passing between Whittle, M‘Gill, and Morris, Gibson got possession, and by a hot shot sent the leather through the posts amidst great cheering and waving of hats. Tkie would have made the score even, but Earlestown claimed that Gibson was off-side, and the referee decided against Everton. The ball was started from the Earlestown goal, but it bad not been kicked half a dozen times, when the referee's whitish) sounded the cessation of hostilities with the score_—
EABLesrown, 1 goal; EVERTON, none.

The scene that ensued alineet bellies description. The ' supperters of the victorious eleven went almost wild in their 1 demonstrations of delight. Amid deafening cheers and , throwing up of hats hucdreds of persons flocked on the field of play, and in a few seconds every member of the Earles- town team was seized and raised shoulder high, and carried amid cheers to the pavilion. On leaving the pavilion and , while making their way across the field, they were still . loudly cheered, and as they drove away from the neigh- bourhood in their waggonette they gave three hearty cheers for their victory. & At Earlestown a very large crowd of persons assembled in the principal streets awaiting the arrival of news giving the result of the cantfet. A rumour was circulated in 901110 quarters that the Earlestonians had been decisively de(eated by five goals to none, but when telegrams began to arrive shortly before six o'clock statiophat the Earlestown "lads" ' had scored a victory after a desperate struggle, there was great rejoicing. Cheers were lustily given for the future ' cupholders, and the news Of the victory quickly spread throeghout the town. There were many anxious inquiries as to when the victorious eleven would return, and it hav- ing been definitely ascertained that they would arrive at Earlestewe oy the ordinary train du,e at ten minutes to eight, a coesiderable crowd .assembled in Queen-street a long time before the train was due, and after half-past seven the street became impassable. On the arrival of the train cortaining the team and a portion of their supporters the street was packed with an enthusiastic throng, who at- tempted to crowd on the platform, but Mr Young, the sta- tion master, and the officials under him judiciously pre- vented this, though the task was one of no small difficulty. The stoppage of the train was the signal for an outburst of prolonged cheers. The enthusiasm was intensified by the discharge of fireworks from the upper part of the premises occupied by Mr B Ktily, tobacconist; and while the de- monstration was at its height three conveyances drove up Iwith difficulty, and in the first of these the members of the team took their seats, upon which the cheers were again re- newed, The players n'cre eabar.quently drivcil 419:g ‘4 iron- streei, Berle-greet, Saukey-eireet, Legh-eireet, Market- street, and up Bridge-street, and they were cheered along the whole route. In return the members of the team gave cheers at the residences or places of business of their most prominent supporters, and at one place some diversion was occesioned by one of their admirers" showering" pork pies upon the players. The team was afterwards Miami. down Queen-street, past the station, and on to the Sunbeam Inn, their headquarters, where they were amply supplied with refreshments. They remained here for the rest of the even- ing, but large numbers of persons stood in groups in the principal streets until a late hour discussing the " points " if the match or speaking in high terms of what was looked upon as a" great victory." in previous stages of the Competition Earlestown has met the following teams:—ln the first round, Birkenhead Argyle, at Birkenhead, was defeeted by six goals to one; the Liverpool Ramblers scratched in the second round; in the succeeding round Skelmeredale were beaten by 5 goals to 0; and in the fourth round (semi-final) Liverpool St. Mary's were thrashed to the extent of 9 goals to 1; total, 20 goals for Earlestown, 2 against. Everton beat Toxteth Wanderers in the first round by 6 goals to 0; in the second round they beat Southport 2to 1; in the next round Bootle were thrown out by 2 to 1; and in the fourth round Got. borne were thrashed by 9 goals to 0; total, Everton 19, opponents 2.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDA jr, MARCH 79 188" FUNERAL OF LIEUTENANT-COLONEL LYON. On Tuesday afternoon, in the Churchyard of Stretton. were laid to rest the mortal remains of the late Lieutenant- Colonel Lyon, ILA., who woo killed by the bunting of a shell at Shoeburyness last week. The particulars of the sad accident on becoming public created a profound feeling of sympathy, and that feeling was intensified in the districts to which the families of those killed belonged. An ex- perimental party, together with some members of the Ordnance Committee of the War office, were experi- menting with sensitive fuses,, and whilst one was being driven into a nine-inch shell, thodatter exploded, inflicting terrible injuries on all who were near. Lieutenant C done! Lyon, who was of the Ordnante Committee, had both legs shattered just below the thigh, and died soon afterwards. He was the son of the late Mr. Thomas Lyon, of Appleton Hall. brother of Mr. Thomas Lyon, the present possessor of the Hall, and brother-in-law of Sir B. A. Cross, G.C.8., who married deceased's sister in 185 Z He held a commis- sion in the Royal Artillery, and was much esteemed as a gallant officer. He had been superintendent of the Royal Laboratory, Woolwich Areenal; since Apra 1880, and had done much to foster the- science of explosives and ordnance., On Saturday the body of the deceased officer was con- veyed from London by special train to Warrington, where it arrived at 9-40 in the evening. IQ attendance at the sta- tion were Major HamiltonoLieutenante Ritchie and Howe,, and eight colour-sergeants, as a guard of honour from Orford Barracks, and by them theooffin was borne from. the train to the hearse, by which le was convoyed to Appleton Hall. As it had become generally known that the funeral would. take place on Tuesday afternoon, a large number of people walked to Stretton Chnrch in a chiaaling rain and ea a miry road to pay their last tokens of respect. Many also drove in nibs and other vehicles, and most of the neigh- bouring gentry either drove to the church or walked in Oee procession from Appleton Hall. Bridge-street, Warring- ton, during the afternoon was literally lined with people watching the passing of the vehicles and the contingent of local volunteers that was in attendance. By three o'clock the churchyard and the adjacent thorough- fares were filled with people, who waited, listening to the mournful tolling of the bell, until about four o'clock, when the funeral proeesssion approached the church. The coffin was covered with the red ensign, and was carried by eight men frem Woolwich, in uniform, members of the late Colonel's regiment, but otherwise the funeral was not of a distinctly military character, as the attendance of a band and firing party were dispensed with. Drawn up in line at , the entrance to the church were about sixty members of the I Warrington corps of the Nor.h Lancashire Rifle Volunteers, under the command of Major Litton, with Lieutenants Gooch and Buckton. The coffin was met at the gate by the Rev. Prebendary Clayton, Rector of Ludlow, first cossin of the deceased, who ponducted the service in the church, which was choral. The hymn "Through the night of doubt and sorrow " was sung as the coffin was borne from the church to the grave. The Rev Prebendary Clay- ton, assisted by the Rev Canon Dodd, vicar of Stretton, officiated at the graveside, and after the coffin had been lowered by the artillerymen from Woolwich, the surpliced choir sang the hymn commencing "My God, my father, while I stray," the assembled people standing with bared heads during the whole of the solemn ceremony. Moss, white flowers, ivy, and lillies covered the sides ef the grave ; on the adjacent graves were Placed wreaths, and wreaths were reverently placed on the coffin when it was consigned to tho grave. The pall bearers were :—Major-General A Pearce, late R.A., Major-General the Hon G T Devereux, late R A., Major-General H A Smythe, HA., Lieutenant- Colonel * P Lynes, R.H.A., Lieutenant-Colonel the lion R V Dillon, RA., Colonel F Anley, HA., Colonel M le Fer Taylor, R A., and Colonel F U it tvenhill. R 4.4, The cilia mourners were :—Mr T H Lyon (brother of the de- ceased), Mr C Lynn, R.A , Mr F Lyon, Mr A Lyon, and Mr H Lyon (sons of the deceased), the Hon Mrs F Lyon (widow of deceased), the Misses M and F Lyon (daughters of deceased), Mrs T H Lyon, Viscount and Viscountess Valentia, Sir Richard and Lady Cross, Mr H Cross, Mr J Crow, the Rev F Cross, Mr Cecil Parr, the Rev Ff. Clay- ton, Mr John Lyon and Mr Ed ward Lyon (cousins), Miss Nangle (niece), Mr Piers Egerton Warburton' M.P., and Mr Uesher. Following them in order of procession were Major Hamilton and officers and non-commis- sioned officers from Orford barracks. A num- ber of the tenants also joined the procession. Amongst those present in the church were Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, Mr Edward and Mr Gilbert Greenall, Mr John White, Mr J Marson, Captain E J Nicholson, Mr Charles White, Mr Sankey, and a number of Aldermen and Councillors of the borough of Warrington. Wreaths were presented by the following :—Officers of the School of Gun- nery, Shoeburyness ; The Woolwich Home for Working Boys, Miss Popham, and the Woolwich Branch of the Guild of St. Helena ; Colonel Markham, RA. ; Colonel and Mrs Anley, Colonel and Mrs Revenhill, Captain and Mrs Hamil- ton, the Rev Canon and Mrs Dodd (cross), Lady Valentia, the Misses Cross (cross), Mrs T H Lyon, Mrs Wilson Fox (cross), the Misses Drake, Mrs Macdonald, Mrs Ussher (cross), Mrs H A Smythe, Mrs Edward Lyon, and Mrs Dyke-Acland. The coffin, which was of oak, with brass mountings bore the inscription : " Francis Lyon, Colonel Royal Artillery, died 27th February, 1885." THB SHOEBORYNBSS PXPLOSION. Mr. Harrison, coroner for South Eesex, opened an official inquiry, on Saturday, touching the deaths of the six sol- diers who have succumbed to the injuries which they re- (reload in the disaster which took place on the marshes ad- joining Shoeburyness Barracks on Thursday afternoon. The evidence taken was only of a preliminary character, and the proceedings were adjourned until Friday. The jury were addressed at some length by the Coroner. Haying detailed I the facts already published, he said that everybody would agree that the deceased officers and men died in the Ber- -1 vice of their country. He proposed that day to view the bodiee, after which the jury would go to the spot where the , accident occurred, and would thence return and take formal I evidence of identification. During the inspection of the Iscene of the disaster it was observed that certain portions of the spot close by where the shell exploded were still sat- urated with blood. Portions of the shell were sent in every direction, large pieces being blown away from neighbouring gun carriages, and, in fact, a portion struck and entered the building over 40yds. away from the spot. Ills said that the cause of the accident was the insertion of the fuse the wrong side upwards. Shortly after the inquest the body of Colonel Lyon was removed to the Shoeburyneas Railway Station, and conveyed by special train to London, en route for Warrington. The procession to the station was of the most impressive character the roadway being lined for the most part with non-commissioned officers of the garrison and horse-artillery. The coffin, conveyed on a gun carriage drawn by six horses, was covered with the Union Jack, sur- mounted with many wreaths of flowers. Upwards of 200 non-commissioned officers and men followed in procession. All military music was suspended in the Woolwich disirict, and the 2nd Kent Artillery Volunteers, who on Sunday at- tended St. John's Church, Plumstead, marched to and from church with the band silent. At most places of worship in Woolwich sermons were preached on the subject of the dis- aster and prayers offered for the survivors and the afflicted families.

THE NEW WESLEYAN CHAPEL, SANKEY BRIDGES. OPENING SERVICES. On Monday afternoon the handsome Wesleyan Chapel just erected at Sankey Bridges was opened, in the presence of a very large congregation. This new chapel is situated on the side of the high road to Liverpool, and, though not large, it is a very elegant construction. The elevation fronting the highway is graced by a beautiful stained glass window which has been put in as a memorial to the late Mr (Sandy, of Penketh, by his sons, who are in the United , States. The theme which this window has been designed to illustrate is "The glory of the Cross of Christ." In the centre of the window stands the emblems of the cross cut , in rosy onyx glass of great purity, and twined around it is the crown of thorns, from which radiate rays of light. This design is enclosed by a field of greenish-blue irridescent glass of a semi•opaque character, across which is thrown an open scroll nt turquoise blue, upon which is read in bright letters the text, "God. forbid that I shall glory save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ," the word "Cross " being, however represented by the emblem of the cross. Surrounding this is a wide border of yellow opal glass of great depth of colour graded in tone from the base of the window to the top. Set in this are masses of incrusted jewels in blue, gold, and opal, which have been hewn with the hammer out of solid masses of glass; and give a high quality of light to the border. The whole design is of the simplest character, a mass of glowing colour calm and re- poseful without distraction or sensation. There is not a particle of paint on the window, all the gradation of tone having been produced by careful selection of the various glasses. Beneath the window is placed a brass plate on which is inscribed, "In memory of John Gandy, Sunny- side, Penketh, born November 14th, 1824, died October 13th, 1882, the above window is erected. It was made in Cincin-1 natti, U.S.A., and placed here by his sons, February, ISM."' The window, it may be mentioned, is altogether of Ameri- canworkmanship, and was designed by one ef the late Mr Gandy's sons. The interior of the chapel is exceedingly light, cheerful, and well ventilated, and will accommodate about 300 persons. I‘.‘e architect was Mr W Owen, of Warrington, and the builders Messrs Gibson and Son, con- tractors, Warrington. The opening service commenced at three o'clock, and prior to that time the chapel was crowded in every part. The preacher was the Rev Charles Garrett, who, before eommencing his discourse, congratulated them very hear- tily on the pleasant day, and on their being permitted after a great deal of anxiety, care, and labour, to take possession of that very commodious house of prayer. He prayed that the blessing of God might be upon them continually, and that they would possess the true spirit of Methodism as well as the true spirit of Christianity. In the old place of wor- ship they were pre•eminent for their earnestness and hearti- ness; let them take care not to let these disappear under the influence of a new and more pretentious place of worship Let thwe who came there never forget that they were in a Methodist chapel. The pulpit would be guarded by the Confereece, but they must guard the pew. There was much that was encouraging about that place of worship, and he had no doubt that all of them felt interested in the dear young men who had so thoughtfully and generously given them

that very beautiful window. He had received a letter from Mr Gandy that morning, in which be said," We shall be thinking abeut you and praying for you when you are met on Monday afternoon, and we trust the blessing of God will be upon yo" Might God bless them wherever they were. They had remembered God'a house and God would newer forget them. It was a comfort to some of them that though God took the father He raised up the children. It was indeed a Bourse of comfort that those children had the same heart and disposition to do. the same werk as that which characterised the life of the father. He was glad to see that the window contained the cross and not the cruci- fies. The cross from the beginning had been the emblem of victory. Theirs Was- not like the Romanist or the High Churchman; they had not a dead Christ. Their Christ was gone, and there was the empty cross, and when they lcoleed upon it it woultl, remind them not of work, vet to be-done bat of a fitaished work. Mr Garrett then selected as- his text the latter part of the 2nd verse of Psalm "Let the children of Zion be joyful in their King,' from which he preachalan eloquent and earnest sermon. In the evening a public meeting was held in the chapel, nhich was again crowded. The chair was taken by Mr Charles Mitchell, of Liverpool, and there were also present the Revs T Rippon (Preston), J McTurk, G E Cutting, W H Jones, W Mules and E Moore; r Gornall, Messrs R Garnett, D Garnett, teamont, Summeregill, Brown (Lynam), Ashton (Lymm), J Walker (Earlestoven), and others.—Mr Surnmersgill read a financial statement from which it ap- peared that prior to that opening service £BOl 175 3d had been contributed towards the cost of the chapel. This sum included several large donations from Mr J Guest, £5O ; Dr Gornall, £5O; Mrs. Coop, £5O; Mr Garnett, £5O; Mr E .1 Guest, £25; Mr Carter, £25; Mr D Garnett, £25; Mrs Garnett, £2O ; and Mrs R Garnett, £25. At the opening service in the afternoon they had received £62 17s 48 —(applause)—and they hoped that before the day was out they would realise £lOO. They had to raise altogether £l3OO, but after they had raised £.1C03 the chapel com- mittee would giva them £3O and lend them £lOO free of in- terest. (Applause.)—The Rev 3 McTurk then read notes of apology for non-attendance from the Mayor and the Hee- J Calvert.—After a short address from the Chairman, the Rev E Moore congratulated the Wesleyans of Sankey Bridges upon having been able to erect to beautiful a sanctuary for the worship.of God. He looked forward with confidence to the good time they would have in the future in connection with that place, and he felt sure that there would be no mistake as-to the sound that would go forth from that pul- pit. .(Hear, hear.)—The Rev W Mules expressed his plea- sure at being there, and said he had not so soon forgotten old associatimas as not to enjoy a meeting weere the building al most, as it were, became ignited with Methodist fire.. Ile thanked them very much far giving him the pleasure and the privilege of expressing his sympathy with t4eln In the work in which they were engaged, and he congratulated them upon the opening of their new place ofeworship. He had not lived within so short a dis- tance of Senkey Bridges for three years without hearing of the noble self-sacrifices which they had been called upon to make from time to time. (Hear, hear, and applause )—Mr. R. GA,RNETT referring to the services of the Rev. T. Rippon in connection with that chapel, said there was no doubt that Mr. Rippon did a very substantial amount towards pushing forward the chapel scheme. (Applause.) He (Mr. Garnett) was glad to see that place, as he had looked for- ward to it with a good deal of anxiety for many months. The friends of Sankey Bridges had done nobly throughout all the sacrifice, labours, and efforts which had been dis- played in connection with that building. He considered it was a sensible building, and one that had been economi- cally built, and not expensive to be kept up, and there was a window in it the like of which they certainly had not in Lencatalaire, in fact he should almost think they had not the like of it in England. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. McTurk then read a letter from Mr. J. R Gandy, in which he referred in sympathetic terms to the work being done at Sankey Bridgee.—Tbe Uri% T. RIPPON7 whe was received with prolonged applause, next addressed the meeting in a speech which was frequently and heartily applauded. He said they had had some trying anxious times in connection with the building of that chapel. They bad a struggle at the quarterly meeting, but their friends stood nobly by them- and they got the scheme launched, and the foundation stone laying was a red letter day in their history. Now ,they had got the building, aad from his heart of hearts he washed them every success. (Applause.) Th et chapel had not been built in any spirit of hostility to any other ceurch, or from any spirit of self-glory or aggrandisement. (Hear, hear.) Now that they had got that new chapel they ought to make it a point of departure, just like youug people who set up housekeeping, seek to make their house beautiful and clean, and just as business firms having gone into new premises seek to do a better work. (Applause.)—A. vote of thanks to the chairman was then moved by Mr. Walker, of Earlestown, which, having been seconded by Mr. Brough and accorded, the meeting soon after terminated. In the course of the evening several anthems were sung by the choir.

div.head: PROTEST BY EVERTOR.
div.p: PROTEST BY EVERTOR.

After the match on Saturday, the Everton Club protested against the decision of the referee (Mr. Hull), with respect to the goal alleged to ha N e been scored by Everton in the last minute of the game. The referee, who was supported by the umpires, declined to allow the point on the ground that Gibson W 33 " off-side " when he shot the leather through the posts. Everton, however, maintained that the point was a legitimate one, and brought the question before the committee of the Liverpool and District Association at a meeting of the latter at the Neptune Hotel, Liverpool, on Thursday evening. There was a full attendance of the com- mittee. An objection was first taken by the Earlestown Club representative, who held that the Everton Club bad not complied with the rules in sending in the protest, hut this point was over-ruled by six votes to four. The com- mittee then proceeded to consider the protest, and after an animated discussion a resolution was passed that the protest be not sustained, and that the referee's decision be upheld. was'carried by six votes to four. Earlestown thus be- come holders of the trophy for 12 months, and absolute owners of handsome gold medals. A large crowd of persons assembled near Earlestown station on Thursday night, awaiting the return of the Earlestown Club representatives with the decision of the Cam mittee. and when the favourable result became known hearty cheers were given.

Four iota/national fixtures under the dribbling code are arranged to take place in March, and the last one, between Wales and Ireland, on the 4th of April; whilst the semi- final and final ties of the national challenge cup competi- tion are to be played on the 7th and 28th instant respec- tively. The success of England in tha Association match against Ireland at Whalley Range an Satarday was looked on as a foregone conclusion, the only interest felt being as to the progress the score would show the Irish players to have made when compared with that of previous years. Viewed in this light the match was satisfactory, as four goals only were scored by England, against thirteen, seven, and eight respectively in the previous three matches. The failure to play the Rugby Union international match at Belfast on Saturday last, owing to boisterous weather, has led to an arrangement being come to under which the match is to be played at Edinburgh on Saturday next, the date and venue of the contest Ciat should have been played between England and Scotland. The first round of the model Yorkshire Rugby Union .Challenge Cup competition was commenced on Saturday, and will be continued weekly to its close. The two most im- portant ties resulted in Bradford throwing out Hull by three goals and three tries to nil, and Wakefield Trinity beating Thornes by one goal to nil. The other ties were only of local interest.

Secretaries of Football Clam are request to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must he sent to thehead °Bice, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday mornbsg.

RUNCORN 2AD TEAM v. OrGHTRINGTON.—These teams met at Runcorn on Saturday to play off their return mash,. when the game ended in a draw in favour of the home team by one try and six minor point., to Oughtrington one try and one minor point. Cox obtained the try for the home team, while Chantler was also successful for Ought- rington. WARRINGTON CRICKET AND FOOTBALL CLVD S'TOCKTO'N HRATH.—Played on the cricket field at arplev on Saturday, and ended in a victory for Warrington by four geals to nil. Warrington :—Legborn (captain). goal; Rye- son and Iliad, full backs; Warburton and Roberts, half backs; Tinnion and Burgess, right wing; Clarke and Critchley, left wing; Burgess and Shaw, centre. WESTON TAM-O'-SHANTERS v. LATCHFORD TRUE BLUES, —Played at Latchford on Saturday, and resulted in an easy victory for the Shanters. Score Shanters, 1 goal, minor points'; Latchford, 2 minor points. Shutters' Team : Fall back, J Green; three-quarter backs, C Pye, P Ragbag, and G A Tudor; ball-backs, P Brookes and U Pendlebury ; forwards, J Farrell (captain), F Dovastoo, T Stringer, W Tudor, A Tudor, W Dean, J Price, A Bennett, and W Wal-

ford. Rusgoner v. WEIINIMEL—PIayed at Wernsth on Satur- day. The ground was in bad condition, and a desultory game resulted. Runcorn scored one try (disputed, pending appeal to the Rugby Union) and two miner points to Wer- neth two miner points. For Runcorn. Lewis, H and W Hughes, and Wainwright all crossed the Werneth line, but the referee decided against the visitors. Teams—Runcorn: WoDds, back; Hughes, Speakman, and Wainwright, three- quarter-backs;. WARRINGTON It. ASPULL.—The return match between these well-known clubs was played at Warrington on Satur- day. Gilbert opened the game, the return being stopped by Massey and Warren. A spirited attack era the Aspull goal was then made and continued for some time, when ensued. some good -passing amongst the home front division, the ball ultimately reaching Barnes, who parted in turn to Mas- sey, this player eff toting a good run in. A second time Aspull were fastened on their line, and from a loose pack Hayes got in between the sticks: the referee, however, ruled it back. some rapid and cross dribbling by the vieitors enabled them to reach centre. and gradually force the ball over the line and score. Pilkington restarted after half time, then play for the first 20 minutes was even. Barnes then madetwersplendid drops, each proving futile, and Warren followed one of them tag and scored, but it was disallowed. The winning point vas secured by Massey, who Was in grand form, as were also Barnes, Warren, Tur- ner, and Rigby. The Aspull backs were only moderate, and of the forwards Hampson, Lawson, and Monks were best. Score : Warrington, two tries and six minor Pleints to one try and three minors. LiyEßrooL AND DISTRICT CHALLENGE CUP. EAELESTOWIT V. 'MERTON. , *THE CUP WON BY EARLESTOWN. Saturday last will remain a red-letter-day for Earles- town. Everyone seemed to have a great interest at stake in the victory or defeat of the Earb-stown Club in the final Us of the competition for the Liverpool and District Asso- ciation Challenge Cup. At the close of last season's com- petition Earlesrown was defeated in the final tie by Everton by the narrow majority of one goal to none, and what is a remarkable coincidence these two crack teams were again left to flat the battle of supremacy this year. But outside the interest attaching to the Challenge Cup, the previous winners of which have been 'Bootle (1882.3), and Everton (1883 4), there were other circumstances which gave the match an importance felt throughout football circles of South Lancashire. It was well lurown there was a keen rivalry between the twe clubs, and that a bitter feeling per- vaded the respective elevens ; and the general opinion was that rather than suffer defeat at the hands of their old op, ponenrs either Earlestown or Everton wuld hare esteemed it a blessing to be thrown drat of the cup contest by the p‘orest team in the district. However, the fates decreed otherwise, and once again the destination of the magnifi- cent trophy and the possession of the handsome gold medals offered by the Liverpool Association rested between the last year's winners and last year's runners-up, or " silver medallists" as they have been popularly termed. From the moment this became known excitement was evinced in Earlestown, Newton, and surrounding districts as to the prospects of the Earlostown team, and the probabilities of the cup findinz a local resting place for at least twelve months. That the match would be a hard-fought one no one doubted, but what was the happiest feature to their sup- porters the Earlestown " lads " came out of the contest with flying colours, and amid the most enthusiastic demon- strations of delight they defeated their poweful and famous opponents by one goal to none—an exact reversal of the score of last year.

Fortunately for the match, the weather was extremely favourable. The sun shone from a cloudless sky, but the atmosphere was nicely tempered with a cool refreshing breeze from the north-east. About two o'clock a special tram left Earlestown Station, conveying some 790 persons to witness the" great match," while a large number of per- sons had travelled on preceding ordinary trains. The Earlestown team took their seats in a specially engaged first•claes carriage of the "special," and as the latter moved 'away on its journey a large crowd of admirers gave ex- pression to their sympathies by hearty cheers and shouts of "Play up, Earlestown." From Lime-street Station to the ground of the Bootle Club in Hawthorne-road, Liver- pool, the Earlestown team was conveyed in a waggonette, and their supporters travelled in trams, 'busses, and other vehicles, while a goodly number walked the distance. The field of play was surrounded by a demonptrative throng—the spectators being four, five, and in some places six deep on all sides. The supporters of the Earlestown team were easily distinguished by wearing in their hats cards bearing the words in red letters "Play up, Earlestown," with a representation of a Maltese cross, symbolical of the " crosses "on the jerseys wern by ths players. It was es- timated that between 5.000 and 8,000 persons were present— by far the largest number that ever attended a football match in the great seaport. The cup-holders first made their appearance, and they were received with applause, but a perfect ovation from all sides of the field awaited the EarlestonianS.

div.head: STORM AT SEA: AN INTERESTING
div.p: STORM AT SEA: AN INTERESTING
IiIARY.

Dr. 3.. H. Gernall, Medical Officer of Health for I Warrington, has supplied us with the following ' interesting extract from his son's diary. The young gentleman, with a view to improving the state of his health, sailed from Liverpool on the 9th October, 1884, in the Gederal Roberts, arriving in Melbourne on New Year's Day. A, few days after rounding the Cape of Good Hope a tremendous storm occurred, and lasted from December ard to Bth. The extract from the diary is as follows :—" December 3. Wind getting pretty strong, moderate gale, and sea running high, waves continually coming over the bulwarks. 12 p.m., fresh gale and high sea occasionally breaking on deck. Vessel rolled tremendously during the night. Thursday, Decem- ber 4th, was a very lamentable as well as a very exciting day. When I began this diary I never thought I should have to ehronicle such a sad event as that which happened to-day. God grant that I may never witness such another. In the afternoon, being troubled with the headache, I had lain myself down in my bunk to sleep. Awoke at 3.30 to find the vessel pitching and rolling awfully, and the sea dashing over the poop. Talk about being rocked in the cradle of the deep,' to-day was too much of a good thing. Presently there was a crash, followed by one ten times greater. My cabin was flooded to the depth of several inches, although the front door of the saloon had been battened up to keep the water out. I sat up on my bunk, as also did Sutton (my Sabin companion), who was asleep on the couch, and began to think matters looked serious. We stared at each other unable to speak or move for several seconds, and then Sutton stepped into the pilot house; and as he opened the door I heard the cry, 'a man overboard.' When I got into the pilot house I found the other pas. sengers with scared faces, who told us that three men had gone overboard. We began to specu- late who the three unfortunates could be, and Miss Pub/ford asked if anyone had seen her brother, and as he did not turn up we began to fear that he was one of them, and it was not long ere this fear became a dread- ful certainty. The ladies went down into the saloon, and the captain shortly afterwards broke the sad news to Miss Pulsford that her brother had been washed overboard. It was for- tunate for me that I was not there at the time, as I was unable to leave the pilot house, being so fascina- ted with the wild sea before me. The captain had , immediately set about bringing round the ship in the hope of picking up the three lost ones; the hal- yards had been cast loose altogether, and the sails were flying about in seeming confusion. The sea all around was one mass of seething foam, and the deck was engulfed by waves mountains high, and at times it was difficult to tell where the sea ended and the sides of the vessel began. The vessel rolled so dread- fully that I thought it would never right itself again. To one unaccustomed to the sea, it seemed a very dangerous thing to bring the vessel round in such a gale with so high a sea. As soon as the vessel got round all hands were mustered on the poop, and I could not help thinking what a picturesque group they looked, some in 'oilskins, some half dressed, two or three in night caps, hair streaming in the wind, all drenched through to the skin, and water steaming from their foreheads with excitement. When they had all assembled the captain asked for volunteers to man a boat. To myself, a landsman, it seemed mad- ness to put out a small boat when even the huge vessel was tossed about like a cork. The words had no sooner left the captain's mouth when up went the third mate's hand, and Here's one, sir,' and Here's another, sir,' and up went the bo'sn's, and this was repeated by a sufficient number of brave fellows to man a boat, although each must have known it would have cost him his life in the attempt. However, they were not called upon to run the risk, as nothing could be seen of the poor fellows who had gone overboard. They were seen from the rigging by one of the crew after the first wave had gone over them, and one of them, John Davies, (A. 8. was seen to have a life buoy, four of which had been thrown out imme- diately. Be waved his hand as if to an eternal fare- well, and after the third wave had gone over them they disappeared. It could not have been morethan /5 minutes before the vessel turned round. As it was going at /2 knots an hour, this spears well for the promptitude displayed. As nothing further could be done, the vessel was brought round on her course. The three poor fellows drowned were IPulsford, one of my fellow passengers in the saloon, a fine looking young gentleman of 24 ; G. Garston, a Yankee, a very typical character, about 45, who had £7O which he carried sewn in a belt round him; and J. Davies, Rhuddlan, near Rhvl, a man who was going to settle in Australia, and was working his passage out. The latter had a brother on board who was terribly cut up at his brother's death. One of the apprentices went overboard by the main rig. ging and was washed back again several yards fur- ther astern. A stowaway was found hanging on to the side an the sea clinging to a davit. It was lucky

no, more were washed overboard by that tremendous sea. Several had hair-breadth escapes. One passen- ger, Clarke, was sitting along with poor Polsford, and found himself clinging to the rails on the bridge. , The second mate standing near the poop steps was ; washed to the top. An apprentice standing on the ; deck was washed into the peep; and nearly over- board. An iron bar on the main hatch was bent double, and anything that was loose was washed away._ The wave that did all the damage was a very high, one, being higher than the top of the jigger mast when it broke on deck (40 feet).. It came up on the stem and over the bulwarks OD both aides. Great damage was done in the steward's department, and as you, can imagine, the rest of the day was intensely miserable, the saloon and cabins being full of water, which swished about with every roll of the vessel, making a very doleful noise. Hats, slippers, ece., &c., ifoated about like the pendulum of a clock, and all we could do was to lament the sad fate of the three unfortunates now left miles behind in their watery grave. It may be well to say that Palsford had been warned of tlfte danger he was incurring, but he said he did not think there was anything to fear but a wetting, which he said was great fun. After dinner he came into our cabin, dressed as if to defy the elements, and asked Mr. Sutton to go out with him to witness the spectacle. He said the waves Wen. breaking on the deck splendidly, but Sutton do. dined. Such a sad day I shall not soon forget."

A SUGGESTION. Sir.—.A report is going the round of Warrington to the effect that the " picture " of a well-known Conservative alderman, which adorned one of the walls of the billiard room at the Conservative Club, met with a serious accident by coming in contact with the boot of a member of the club a few evenings ago. May I be permitted to suggest to a certain councillor that he would do a gracious act by pre- senting to the club a span new " picture ' of the aforesaid alderman, the frame to be made by his own hands, and turned out in his best style of workmanship.—Yours, Jac., March 5, 1885. A LOVER OF PICTURES. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH. Sir,—l was much pleased to see the able little leader in your last issue bringing before the public the nnniber of curates who have come and gone during our present Rector's regime; but I think that in putting the number down at 68 you are much below the mark. I believe that the Revs. Corey and Mitchell made over three score and ten ; and, as it is just over twelve months since we had to part with those two able ministers, you will see that those in power have not been idle when, during the year that has elapsed, we have had the Revs. Joeynd, McGonigle, Wright, Ward, and Montgomery; also about two who stopped so long that I could not get their names before they were off again. Besides these rev, gentlemen going, our late esteemed organist, Mr. Rowley. and his choir have been pensioned off with the usual allowance of back-biting, for which they are of course thankful; and now I hear that the Rev. Mr. Weller is about to take his departure. If there is not something radically wrong in tne treatment to which' these have been subjected, I think the Rector utust have dropped on some very bad servants. What is the parish- ioners' warden doing? Why does he not call a public meeting of parishioners to deal with thess things.—Yours respectfully,
A PARISMONER.

Sir,—lt appears strange to me that in your cllumne you should so repeatedly allow others and yeiarself to attack the Rec'or of the Warrington Parish Church. If, before writing your article in last Saturday's Examiner, you had eought an interview with the Rector respecting the subject upon which you dwelt, he would, I think, have given you tar better information respecting the leavireg of the last curate than you seem to possess; and after hearing his explana- tion, you will excuse my bo'dness in saying that you would not have penned that article. But why these attacks upon the Rector, a man over eighty years of age ? The noble work that he has accomplished throughout his life is de- serving of all our respect, and that respect was shown to him not long ago by placing his bust by subscriptions in the Art Gallery'. Well, sir, there are curates and there are curates ; but the people of Warrington cannot pry into their past lives, better they cannot, but before passing judgment upon an incumbent er rector, they should first ascertain the reasons of their parting with their curates. But that is not a question I care to dwell upon I wish to speak of the Rector's doings. Well, I will take one example only, the restoration of the Parish Church. That accomplishment alone should suffice and gain for the old gentleman the highest esteem and regard of the people of Warrington. How beautiful it is to assemble in that noble edifice without money and without price except what you like to give ! Tours respectfully, D.

TEETOTALISM IN EARLESTOWN. 4ir,—Just a few lines in reply to " Moderator's " remarks on the" new whoa" theory, the main point in his letter of last week. First, the Jews, in the time of Christ, after 1,500 years' experience in fermenting wines, were not se ignorant of chemical science as to attempt to carry on fermen:ation of grape juice in skin bottles tightly closed at the mouth. It is a certain fact, not a mere opinion, that, as easily as frozen water bursts leaden pipes in winter, wine whilst fer- menting will burst the strongest skin bottle ever made, whether of ox or goat hide, or even the akin of the invul- nerable rhinoceros. It has been known to burst even iron- bound casks. In proof of this, I beg to refer " Moderator " to two of the highest anti-abstaining authorities on vine culture—friends, defenders, and improvers of wine manu- facture, Drs. Thudicum and Dupre., who show very plainly that the extensive force liberated by fresh grape juice when undergoing fermentation is enormous. They state that a must, ore-fifth sugar, developes 47 times its volume of car- bonic dioxide, equivalent to a nressure of 34.3 atmospheres, or equal to 500Ibs. on the square inch, which is about ten times the pressure an ordinaryhigh-pressure steam engine has to withstand. That this immense pressure, which would re- sult from the fermenting of unfermented grape juice, would burst bottles asunder is a phenomenon very easily under- stood, and of this fact the Jews could not but have full knowledge.

- But not only does chemical science support the explana- tion I have previously given of the" new wine skins," it is also confirmed by ancient and present custom. Dr. Eli Smith, in his "Bib. Sacra.," says,—" In Lebanon the grapes are pressed, and to bring about fermentation the must grape juice is put into open jars. In Palestine, as in France and other parts of Europe, it is common to carry on the fermentation of must, by free exposure to the air—not in air excluded skin bottles or vessels—for then the sealed up vessels would certainly burst,a fact I have already very clearly shown." As to present custom, an application for information to any one acquain- ted with the process of brewing will no doubt elicit the fact that it is customary for beer, much more wine, to be fermented in open vats. In the face of the above facts, what becomes of the opinions of his authorities, Archbishop Trench and Burdillon. Like Professor Eadie, who follows in the same track, they were evidently unacquainted with chemical science, or they would never have given expres- sion to such conflicting opinions.

And now, Sir, in Conclusion, I was not surprised to find that " Moderator " concluded by stating be will in one short letter give his reasons for thinking Christ was not an abstainer, thus virtually acknowledging his foundation te be one of theory, not of fact. What a falling off is there f And yet one cannot blame Moderator.' Better men than he have many times before attempted the same thing, and like him have utterly failed. All they can do Is simply barricade themselves behind their own peculiar opinions. It would certainly have been much better if "Moderator' had started from that standpoint at the first instead of attempting to prove an impossibility. If he had, the probability is that he would have had the field to himself, as there could be no benefit to be derived in a dis- cussion where an "historical fact" is to be propped up by mere opinions However, I shall be glad to, read "Modera- tor's" reasons for thinking Christ was not a testotaller.—l am, yours respectfully, TEE TEE. Earlestown, 4th March, 1885.
MR. NORMAN SENR., AND ECONOMY AT RUNCORN.

Sir,—lt must be patent to all careful readers of your last issue that the production of a letter signed "Veracity" caused its author much thought and some trouble. The laboured yet futile attempt to " take a rise" out of me clearly showed this, but if, after a fortnigh't' thought, I could not have put before the public a better defence of Mr. Norman than he has done, I would have refrained from in- truding upon your valuable space. The verbosity—verging somewhat upon exuberance—and phraseology of the effusion clearly point out the author as being "the ccming man," not only in local matters—but in the estimation of his family at least—in nationallaffairs. His first statement, viz., "that without subscriptions, col- lections, or popular entertainments, the managers of the Wesleyan schools promptly discharge their liabilities, and hand over to their trustees-a substantial rent for the build- ing they occupy" much. surprised me. I must dispute this statement with him,.er at least a part of it, as me- thinks I have heard of collections in chapel for the school, and can most positively state that teachers employed in the schools have complained most bitterly of their small pit- tance, and of the length of time they have had to wait for their earnings, even after the Government grant has been received by the managers. But, taking the statement as correct, is it not a fact that the solvency of the school and the munificence of the managers to the trustees are main- tained by charging 2d per head per week, upon at least half the children: in attendance,, over and above the fees charged at other schools in the town ? In addition to the fee of 6d, isn't 3oamething (perhapa 25 per cent) made upon the reading an. 4 other books that the children have to chase ? Hera, Mr. Editor, we have another instance of a class of people posing as ardent educationalists so tong as something can be wrung out of poor people in support of a denomination. Only fancy, a high fee to shield them from subscriptions, entertainments, collections, and to enable them to hand over to their trustees "a substantial rental." I trust that the consideration of these facts—they are quota- tions from the letter of "Veracity "—by those whom the Education Act was framed to benefit, will show that in pay- ing the increased fee, parents are in reality supporting the denomination in general. Having to my own mind—puny 1 humbly adistit--.de- Inolished " Veracity's " accusation of misrepresentation on Wheel matters, I beg to be allowei t Wei in, A few sea-

The joiners' shop has been fitted as a mortuary. and men were engaged all day making coffins for the recep- tion of the bodies as they are recovered. On Wednesday the work of exploration was continued, but owing to the heavy "falls" which had to be penetrated no considerable progress was made. Only one body was reached. No hope is entertained that the entombed miners have survived the explosion and its after affects. Seventy horses and ponig have been killed. It is now prac- tically certain limit 40 men have lost their lives by the disaster.

div.head: DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.

At Bow-street Police Court, London, OR Monday, James G. Cunningham and Henry Burton were again charged before Sir James Ingham with being concerned in causing tne explosion at the Tower on January 24th. Mr. Poland prosecuted the prisoners on behalf of the Treasury, and Mr. Quilliam, of Liverpool, defended.—Mr. Poland, in open- ing the proceedings, said they had ascertained that the two prisoners were in New York last December, Burton remain- ing there until the 17th of that month, and the other pri- soner till the 1011, arriving there on the 20th. Having so arrived, Cunningham had stayed for three days at Liver- pool, the Oregon arriving on the next day with Burton. Afterwards he left for London with the brown American trunk. Evidence would be called from Liverpeol on the subject connecting the two prisoners together, and it would be proved that Cunningham brought the trunk from Liver. pool to Broad-street. The possession of the trunk connected Burton and Cunningham together. On February 20th last year Burton arrived from New York at Southampton in a German vessel called the Donan. While staying at South- ampton he had purchased a portmanteau. He left Southamp- ton for London, and on the 25th of February a plan had I been prepared to blow up four of the principal railway stations in London, the Victoria Station, the Ludgate Hill Station, the Paddington Station, and the Charing Cross Station of the South-Eastern Railway. The plan was to pack portmanteaus or boxes with Atlas dynamite fu cakes, labelled " Atlas Powder A," by means of this powder, which was dynamite of a powerful character, and manufac- tured at Philadelphia. The plan was to pack about 21lbs in each of the portmanteaus, and to delay the explosion for a time by means of clockwork. The alarm clock was so arranged that at a particelar hour it would act in the trig- ger of a pistol and fire it. The flame from the mouth of the pistol would act on the detonators, and the detonators going off would explode the 2111) of dynamite. That plea was proved conclusively, for three of the portmanteaus deposited in the left luggage offices had been found unexploded. At Charing Cross a portmanteau was foend which would be • clearly identified as having been bought by Burton at Southampton after his arrival in the Donan. Among the passengers was a person giving the name of Edward Eolton, who, be believed, was the prisoner. In the portmanteau were several newspapers dated February 21st, and about seven o'clock on the 25th the portmanteau was deposited at Charing Cross. Burton, while at Southampton, was wear- ing a coat which had been noticed at the time, and half of a coat similar to it had been found in the portmanteau discovered at Charing Cross. There was further evidence that Burton, after returning to the United States, came back to We country on May 16. There was the curious coincidence that the three machines having failed a new scheme was adopted. On May 30 there was the explosion at Scotland-yard. Another on the same night at Sir Wat- kin Williams-Wynn's house in St. James's-quare, and another at the Junior Carlton Club. They were not done with machinery, and it appeared that the stuff was carried to the different places and explodeel by a time fuse. A bag, already packed for the purpose of a fourth explosion, had been found on the night of the explosion at the base of Nel- son's Column. In the bag was the Atlas powder Ato the amount of 81be, and the fuse and detonators ready to be ex- ploded. After referring to other explesiene, the learned eOuneel called evidence from Liverp66l, which fully bore Out his statement as to the contents of Burton's portmanteau— The inquiry was then adjourned. At Bow-street, Load on, en Tueeday, the charges of treason felony against the pri- soners Burton and Cunningham were resumed. Several witnesses from Southampton identified Burton as arriving there in the steamer Donau in February last year, and pur- chasing several portmanteau, one of which was found at Charing Cross Station containing dynamite. A witness named Bennett positively identified Burton as the man who bought the portmanteau produced (the one found at Char- ing Cross with an infernal machine in it--The case was adjourned until Monday next.
