div.head: -OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: -OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON', TAURSDAY. For a bai quarter of an hour, between a quarter past one and half past, on Saturday merning, it seemed as if England for its sins was about to be plunged into the blackest disaster that could reach it. The Conservatives had whipped up their available men is order to carry the Vote of Censure. The halt, the lame, and the blind were there, , all eager to inflict a blow upon the Minister whom they with good political reason bate. The Faroeßites had been equally assiduous, and more than usually fortunate. The thirty-two votes with which in May last they had swelled the Opposition host as now increased to forty- four. Mr. Goschen and Mr. Forster bad walked out •to vote for Lord Salisbury against Mr. Gladstone. Ten other gentlemen who sit for Liberal constituencies and •Yote with Tory faction had gone the same way. It seemed almost impossible that the Liberals could muster sufficient to hold the bridge that led to the coveted seats on the Treasury Bench. A triumphant majority was outside all calculations. The question was—would there be a safe one?

Mr. Gladstone made an heroic endeavour to appear un- Concerned, writing a letter amid the bustling of members streaming in from either side the division lobbies. But it was a pretence that would not last, and after a while he shut up the unfinished letter and sat watching with flushed face and weary eyes the gathering throng that ever poured In from the doorway under the clock, a motley company of constitutional Tories, obstructive Irishmen, factions Whigs, and disappointed ex-Ministers. Sir Charles Dilke and Mr. Chamberlain joked and chatted with unaffected merriment. Personally a defeat of the Government would have been very acceptable to them. It meant an opportunity for Lord Salisbury and his friends to demonstrate their inability to govern, and to sheer how much easier it is to criticise than to work. Resignation just now would relieve them from many embarrassments; would free their hands and prepare their way for a return to power in a few months with greatly added strength. So they gaily chatted whilst fr m one end of the House and the other, from under the clock facing the chair, and from the wide passegcs behind the chair, members constantly poured in. It was just half-past one when the result was made known, And a triaMphant cheer burst from the Liberal ranks. Fourteen seems a small majority for the captain of such a host as five years ago the ceuntry placed at Mr. Gladstone's back. But 14 was more than Liberals had dared to hope for, and more than Censervatives had presumed to expect. By a mental calculation universally undertaken and swiftly accomplished, it was seen that the Ministerial majority was actually 53. However the Irish vote had gone, it would, by common consent, have been deducted from the figures as having no actual bearing upon the merits of the question, Or upon the Position of the Ministry. Weat Mr. Parnell wanted to do was ta embarass the Ministry, and, if possible, bring about a deadlock. If they had brought the Conserva- tives in on Saturday morning, they would have voted against the new Government on Monday. It illustrates the abnormal condition of political affairs that there ehould have been talk of resignation, and that Ministers themselves should eareestly have considered the subject at the Cabinet Connell. Never beforeednceConeti- tntional Government began was there question of whether a Government will a majority of 14 should resign, and this was the cash of Ministers with a practical majority of 53. However the figures be looked at, they bring out results fatal to any supposition of a serious weakening of the Government. In May laet year, the last time a fall of this kind was tried by the Opposition, 303 Liberals voted with Mr. Gladstone. On Saturday there were 302, and half a deem reamers of Liberels absent through eircum- stances over which they had no control—Sir W. Lawson for example, Lord Lymington, and Colonel Kingcote—sug- gest themselves to account for the diminution of one. Much is made of the fact that in May the majority was 23, whilst on Saturday it was only 14. Bet this is easily accounted for. The Parntlites pored twelve more, and Mr. Forster and Mr. Goscben, finally ending their tortuous coarse by arriving in the Conservative camp, voted with the Parnell- , ite•Tory coalition. However much personal inclination may have drawn the Cabinet towards resignation, it was Impossible for them with any sense of public duty to choose the easier path. So they remained, and will doubtless re- main through what is left of thia session, hampered and pestered on every side by the political combination' that jest failed to destroy them on Saturday. The interest in affairs in the Soudan has been suddenly and almost completely obscured by a fresh one. A cloud has arisen out of the North, and Russia is discovered Stealthily adveneine on Afghanistan. Tale na,vs, which has so suddenly and unexpectedly burst upon the public, has long been in possession of the Government. Whilit they have been supposed, not without good reason, to have enough on their hands in the Soudan, they have been quietly and, I believe it will turn out, effectually check- mating Russia on the Afghan frontier. Their method of dealing with a crisis of this kind is very different from whet we were familiar with seven or eight years ago. At that petits'', when Lord Beeconkfi lid was Premier, he was always theatrically posing, and amid the clatter of music ball glasses daily declaring that he would die in the breach rather than let Haute tench British interests with plunder- ing finger. The fleet made dremaeic amens upon the Dar- danelles, the order for its advance being immediately • followed by a telegram of withdrawal. There has been nothing of that kind during the last three months. The Public hear of the advance of Russia only at a time when they also learn -that the Czar has been quietly but firmly told that he enters Afghanisten at peril of a war with Eng- laud, a threat effectively backed up by full preparations. Nothing could afforJ more striking proof of tbe statesman- ship which has confronte I Russia at the present juncture than the fact that the Opposition have not been able to utter a single word of a !verse criticism, whilst the Times is graciously patronising to Ministers who have done so well. This is a state of things that should be enjoyed to the full, fur it will not last lung. Trained ingenuity, com- bined with utter recklessness of statement, will soon find opening for cavil. Writing last week about a statement circulated by a special correspondent in the Soudan alleging that the square at Abu Kiel was broken by orders of Colonel Burnaby, I ventured for reasons given to ee-press doubt of the truth of the state- ment. I felt confident that in due time it would be author- itatively contradict* But 1 did not imagine that contra- diction would come so early and so completely from the very source whence issued the false report. Mr. Charles William% who is responsible for the issue of the original statement, gives particulars in a letter published on Toes- lay, which entirely disposes of his own earlier statement. Se fur from Colonel, Burnaby, a staff officer, taking upon -himself at a critical moment to give fatal orders to the Heavies, he now states that Colonel Burnaby proceeded to -the reel' of the square at the instructions of General Stewart; that he found the rear left corner of the square in a state of wild confusion; and that he attempted Co execute a military elancenyre that wtuld have checked the Arabs I had he had the good fortune to have arrived a few minutes earlier. As it 1738 be died galleetly in the front in a per- sonal effort to rally the Guards. Yesterday a still more detailed account of the battle, mo-e particularly Burnaby's share in it, appeared lo the Daily Telegraph. It agrees with Mr. Williams's in the main facts, and, going beyond that account, shows Barnabv eo have lost his own life in the endeavour to cover the retreat of three skirmishers who were driven in by the Arabs. Thee.t. later accounts complete a story that shows military skill, self-devotion, and Smiling courage in the face of danger overborne by numbers. Mr Irving's dramatic cable message to Lord Tennyson asking permission to put " Beckett" on the stage is the answer to Mr. Wilson Berrett's enterprise in producing the posthumous work a Lord Lytton. Mr. Irving has hitherto led the fashionable world, which likes to have its plays done by eminent hands, and he is not disposed to suffer a rival in the field. It is the opinion of some practical dramatists whom I have heard discuss the matter that if "Beckett" is to be Made into a play, it will have to be severely dealt with?. There are one or two scenes which have the dramatic fire in them, notably in the conversation between the King and Beckett, and the scene in which the Queen makes her Way to the bower of Fair Rosary-end. Possibly these two might make the fortunes of a plece,supposing the other acts were made passable. As for "Junius or the Household Gols," it certainly will do nothing to raise the reputation of the author of " Richelies," Lhe " Lady of Lyons," and "Money." I had the pleasure the other day of visiting a lady whose father was a midshipman on board the "Victory," and saw Nelson fall. She has many relics of the time, including a little eneraving of Nelson, which the young midshipman, his morals evidently disturbed by the excitement of the reernent, frankly admits he annexed from Nelson's cabin. To me the most striking, thing was the medal which the midshipman, having had the time given him to glow into a full blown pest captain, received. Trafalgar, as everyone ,knows• was fought in 150,1. Trafalgar medals were issued elne 183% a year after her gracious Majesty cattle to the throne. It is difficult to concsive anything more monstrous than this. A medal and a hit of ribbon are in many cases all that a gallant fellew gets for risking his life and perad- venture losing a limb. But how many who fought at Tra- falgar must have gone to their graves without even having this poor consolation! The Soudan war has involved the illustrated papers in considerable expense. Bat this is one of the cases where extra expenditure judicially laid out leads to fortune. I hear of the dividend jest dLlribuled to the few select share- holders in one of the great weekly illustrated newspapers. It is of the cemfortable syinmetricel proportions of cent per I cent.

NtRDER OE A POLICEVAN —On Sunday night, at Bit.- rain4hani, Moses Shrimpton, an elderly man, and 3 re- turned convict, was arrested an a chary of wilfully mur- dering P.C. Davies, who was found on Saturday morning a few miles from Alyechurch with his throat cut. Upon the prisoner was found a knife st;:ined with blood. When arrested he made no reply to the charge, except that the injuries he had himselfsus`ained had taken place a week since. On medical advica being given it was shown that the injuries must have been inflicted within the previous 24 hours.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ' A monthly meeting of this Conloll was held in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), presiding; Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Davies, Webster; Councillors Broadbent, Ridgway, Roberts, Ashton, Barker, Bolton, Brown, Burgess, Crosfield, Dakin, Dixon, Fleming, Francomb, Greening, Hutchinson, Litton, Mackie, Milner, John Pierpoint, W. Pierpoint, Platt, Ridg- way, Sutton, Taylor, Tinsley, and Wright • Messrs Brook (town clerk), Whittle (depute town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), and Chorley (borough treasurer). A TECHNICAL POINT. The MAYOR moved that the minutes of the Council meet- ing of the 3rd February be taken as read. Alderman WEBSTER said that on the 3rd February a special Council meeting was convened for the purpose of taking into consideration a certain matter. As he under- stood—be did not happen to be present himself—the special meeting never took place, as there was never a quorum, and therefore the matter fell through. It seemed to him, there- fore that the resolution to adjourn which was come to had no effect whatever, because if there was not a quorum he did not see how they could adjourn. The MAYOR said there was a meeting called for half-past five. It was quite true that at half-past five there was net a quorum to deal with a special subject, but there was an ordinary quorum, there were more tban twelve present, and it was proposed that the special meeting should be adjourned until later on when they had a quorum sufficiently large to

to deal with the subject. Alderman WEBSTER maintained that as the special meet- ing bad never been held, there was no power to adjourn it. It fell through as a mitter of course. The Towez CLERK said it was his opinion that the Council had power to adjourn, having the usual quorum of the Council present. Alderman WEBSTER, however, still contended that the Council had no power to .adj nun a special meeting which had never been held. Councillor Meaux called attention to the fact that the legal adviser of the Council had passed a plain and distinct opinion on the subject, and said they were spending the time of the Council in a highly objectionable way. The MAYOR: The Town Clerk has given his opinion, and there is an end of it. Alderman Wraeszen : I enter my protest, because I am satisfied the special meeting was never held. The MATOE : I think you will know that it was held. Alderman WEBSTER : Yes, but the time was gone by; half-past five was the time. Councillor DIXON then seconded the Mayor's proposal, which was carried. THE LATE ALDERMAN TERVILIS. The MAYOR said the next business was the appointment of a successor to the late Alderman Tbewlis. It had been their custom that when a member of that Council had been remeved by death, to notice the event publicly, and to DABS a resoltation of condolence with the friends of the deceased; and also at the same time to express their own regret in a kindly and sympathetic spirit. (Hear, hear.) And it was very proper, he thought, that they should do so when they came to remember that their late friend and colleague was a conspicuous figure in Warriegton for about fifty years past. Conspicuous he might say advisedly; for his own high sense of honour, for his commercial integrity, sad lastly as a good and loyal citizen, lie was a member in that Cauncil as long as to fairly entitle him to the soubriquet of "father of the Council," and be thought there were few who had passed away before him from amongst them who were better entitled to be so spoken of than- the late Alder- man Thewlis. (Hear, hear.) He might tell them that the deceased in his haft will and testament, executed not very long ago, had not forgotten the suffering poor, and they would bs pleased to know that lie had left the sum of £5OO to their excellent Imfirmary. (Applause.) In addition, he had left £5OO, the interest of which was to be distributed each year by his trustees and by the Mayor for the time being to the poor people who stand in need of extra Coin- forte at Christmas time. (Applause) lie might also tell them of another trait in his character. He had left the sum of £5OO, the interest of which was to be devoted to a fund for the support of retired Wesleyan ministers. He con- (ended by rowing a vote of condolence to Mrs. Thewlis. Alderman HOLMES secended, and Councillor Dimes sup- ported this proposal, which was unanimously adopted. THE ELECTION OF AN ALDERMAN. The MAYOR said that in electing a SUCOSSSOf to Alder- man Taewlis it was not absolutely necessary that a formal proposition should be made ; it would be quite sufficient if , each member of the ,Council filled up the name of the gentleman he. chose to vote for and band it up to him. _

Councillor Mau= said although it was not needful that I a formal proposition shoeld be made of any name to fill the vacancy caused, he wished to be allowed to propose a name and to say why he wished to do it in a manner other than that provided by law. In that Corporation, and in many others, the custom bad obtained for a great number of years, that when any councillor had filled the office of Mayor, after his year of office had expired, he should be entitled to, or elected to the first vacant alderman's chair that there might be. That custom had been carried out in the War- ' rington Corporation until within a very few years since. Then, at a time of gre,t political excitement it was departed from, rued be did not know that any single act of that Cor- poration had clued mere trouble than had the departure , from that good custom. A man who had worthily filled the office of Mayor was entitled to occupy the seat at an alderman of the borough; and no one was more fitted to occupy such a seat than the man who had filled the chief office of the Corporation. He took it that the meaning of alderman was " elderman "—the oldest and wisest amongst them—(hear, hear,)--and the man who had the widest expe- rience was the man who ought to be elected to fill that office. He understood that they were to have on that subject that night another party vote, a thing which he extremely re- gretted. (Hear, hear.) The man he was about to propose was a man who agreed with him in politics certainly, and, therefore, it might be said that ha (the speaker) was about to give a party vote, or make a party proposition. He en- tirely denied that. Nothing would give him greater plea- sure than to vote for the gentleman who represented the opposite side in politics when his time came, and when he had passed the chair of Mayor, in due course, if such a vacancy occurred. He was not that night going to vote against Councillor Sutton—(hear, hear,)—as Councillor Sutton. He was going to propose to them the name of a man who had passed the Mayor's chair; and without fur- ther words he begged to propose Councillor John Crosfield as a fit and proper person to be elected to the vacant seat of alderman. Alderman J: DAVIES said perhaps he was the man to speak at this point;, and he did not agree with Councillor Crosfield in politics at all. He should think that in politics no men were wider in their differences tban Councillor John Crosfield and himself; but he wished to make a simple statement to the Council as to the course he was about to take; and he wanted that CORM to be quite independent of anyone else. He was only speaking for himself when he told them what determined him to take the course which he was about to take. In the year 1871—when he was elected Mayor—and in the year 1872 especially he was called upon by Mr. -Cieorge Crosfield, and it was about the time when there seemed to be a gleam of hope of having an opportu- nity of purchasing that Town Hell and grounds around it, and he received much consolation and assistance from Mr Crosfield in attempting to negotiate that purchase—and this at the time when Mr Crosfield-was so strongly opposed to him in politics—and Mr. Crosfield expressed a desire that he should never again let political feeling enter into anything that he did in the Council. And to show that he meant what he said, he promised to subscribe very, very materially to the purcha3e of that Hall and grounds, if he would also take the course indicated. In the year 1873, at a time when it was very likely—very likely indeed—that the purchase would go off altogether, and when as Alder- man Holmes and Councillor James Sutton—who was then with them—knew very well; for if it had not been for those two able men at his interview with Colonel Wilson-Patten at that time, it was possible the whole thing would have been thrown to the winds. He went to Mr. Crosfietd at Walton Hall and he explained the position to him, and he promised to give, if they as Councillors would set aside all political feeling in the Council—fighting as much as they liked outside—he promised first to give £5,000, but on the completion of the purchase £lO,OOO. Of coarse "Whisper- ing Tom " said Mr. Crosfield was acting for political pur- poses, but Mr. Crosfield announced his intention of not op- posing Sir Gilbert Gleenall in the contest of that time. Mr Crosfield acted from purely patriotic motives. Councillor BURGESS : What has that got to do with the election of an alderman? Alderman DAVIES said it had everything to do with the election of an alderman, and he was surprised that any- body should have the audacity or the cruelty to interfere or question it. Councillor BURGESS asked it it was in order for Alderman Davies to use the words he had. The MAYOR thought they were scarcely in order. Councillor BURGESS: Then you will perhaps ask that the words be withdrawn? Alderman Dams said he would withdraw them at once if Councillor Burgess did not like them. He then went on to say that he wished the Council and the world to know that what he had stated had not in any measure hampered him in political matters; for he thought that it would be quite admitted that in 1874 he fought as well for Sir Gil- bert Greenall as any man in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) And subsequently to that time, and especially at the elec- tion of Aldermen Holmes and Burgess, he bad said that he would never be a party to politics in the Council. And notwithstanding the fact that he had strong influence brought to bear upon him he maintained that position, and those men (Aldermen Holmes and Burgess) were returned, to the honour of the Council. He contended that it would have been a mod dishonourable thing if the Council had through a political feeling turned those two men out of the Council. He thought the Council might well be proud of them. When Mr. Crosfield was the Mayor of Warrington, he discharged the duties of the office in a manner second to none, and he was brother to the man who did so much for them previously. Was he (the speaker) going to let party politics interfere with what wag for the l nefit of the Cor- poration, or for the benefit of the towr 2 Certainly not, and therefore he should vote for Council'D Crcfield to be Alderman of the borough, and if he were not elected almost unanimously it would be a lasting disgrace to the borough. Councillor MACKIE said he felt sorry that the quiet method of simply filling up the voting papers had not been adopted. (Hear, hear.) They had all come with their minds thoroughly made up, and Alderman Davies had come with his mind so made up that he had been able to deliver the strongest language which they were accus-

div.head: EXANIINFR, SATURDAY, MARCH 7, 1885.
div.p: THE EXANIINFR, SATURDAY, MARCH 7, 1885.

tomed to hear even in that place. (Hear, bear.) He thought it was a great mistake that Councillor Crosfield should be dragged forward in the way he had been. (Hear, hear.) It was so some two or three yeago, when Alderman Davies did the same thing, quite unnecessarily, at the elec- tion of mayor, and he ventured to say, although he would not presume to claim much of the friendship of Mr. John Gros&id, that his name stood far too high in the town to be made a shuttlecock of by a party when they thought oc- casion presented itself. They were all partizans in that Coun- cil—(hear, hear—when it came to the election of aldermen. He trusted that no such rule as that which had been pro- . . . . ,

_ posed of only electing men who had passed the chair would for one moment be recognised there. But if it were, why not carry it oat fairly? Councillor Broadbent was Mayor before Mr. Crosfisld—(hear, hear)—he was Mayor for one or two years, and Councillor Broadbent was proposed at the last general election of aldermen as a pure party move, if ever there was one. (Hear, hear.) They should not tile of having no party feeling in the matter. They were come not as pirtizens to guage each other, mentally, morally, or physically; but politically, and this was the only reward that men like Councillor Sutton, who bed borne the burden and heat of the day for many years, had to look forward to, and why should it be taken away from them? Alderman Davies had spoken of the election of aldermen three or four years ago. He (Dr. Mackie) was not in the Council then, but he knew that election Was not an election on the fair ground upon which party votes were taken. It returned two able Liberals, but it had done more to smash, not the Mandi, but the Conservative party of Warrington than all the other blunders which had been committed, and they had not been few nor far between. (Hear, hear.) Now he would ask them how had Mr. Crosfield conducted himself as a party man not, under the guidance of his respected brother —whose name never would be uttered by him but with re- spect—(hear, hear)—not under the guidance of his brother, for he did not believe he was ever coneulted in the matter I' Councillor Crosfield did not think it beneath him as a party move to try to keep one of the wards of Warrington which, wished to sand him (Dr Mackie) into the Council without its representative on the trumpery plea that he (Dr. Mackie) was three or four months out of the town too long to render him legally entitled to enter the Council. In consequence of this he had to wait for one or two years, simply because he, who had lived in the town then more than 20. years, had for a time been living out of it. He ventured to say that parties must exist in this country, in the Senate House, and in the Town Council, and on those grounds he bad very great pleasure in proposing Councillor Thomas Sutton as alderman, and he would have been equally willing to pro- pose any other gentlemen whom the party had been pleased to'select. (Hrar, hear.) Alderman WEBSTER said he had not the slightest doubt that the name of Crag:laid would always be respected in Warrington, and in the Council, and he should have been pleased if it had been in his power to have supported Coun- cillor John Crosfield, but he expressed his intention of sup- porting Councillor Batton. Councillor Boalarss said that Alderman Davies had in- dulged in *long panegyric of Mr. George Crosfield; still he had not said one word but what was deserved, and if he had said as much of Mr. John Crosfield he (the speaker) would have been prepared to endorse every word. (Hear, hear.) He thought be could not too thoroughly explain that on that matter he did not pretend to be voting for a person, bat be did intend to vote for his party. (Applause.) Be thought it was a very unfortunate thing that the usual custom had been departed from that night, but ha supposed the course pursued had been adopted in order to give a certain gentleman the opportunity of saying why he had determined to sell his party. He (Councillor Burgess) entered the Council as a Consirvative, and would never have been returned had he not been e Conservative. He should vote for Councillor Sutton because he was a Con- servative. and treated Councillor Sutton would be elected because he was a Conservative. (Hear, hear.) . Councillor Maxus entirely repudiated the suggestion that he had got up to speak to allow a gentleman to explain why he was going to "sell his Patty." Councillor BURGESS' said he would withdraw anything that seemed to reflect upon CoUncillor Milner. Alderman DAVIES here explained that he understood that the councillor to be elected in the place of Councillor Crosfield would not be opposed by the Liberal party. Ctuncillor Pearr said he would ask was it fair to the Liberal party in the Coencil that because they had a minority of one vote in Council matters, standing as 14 Cosservitives to 13 Liberals, 14 councillors should be re- premnted by seven aldermen and the Liberals by only two aldermen ? (Cries of " No" and " Yes.") He would in- vite the Conservatives to r,ctify that arrangement by giving to the party entitled to it their share of aldermen. Further than that, he should say that the Conservatives had their majority In the Council by a mere accident, frcol fact that the wards of the barough were 110 t equally divided. (Loud cries of Hear, hear," and "No, no)') They owed their majority to the fate that the wards were most unfairly divided ia the town. They bad been invited , on one previous occasion to rectify this state of things, which was admitted to be unjust in Liverpool and other great towns. The first time it was brought forward it was carried ha the Council that it was to be altered, but su'eae- quemly it was found by the Tory party that it would be detrimental to their interests, and consequently the question was shelved. The party In the town was not fairly repre- sented in the Council, and gentlerrien who voted on the first occasion fot the re-arrangement of the wsrds voted on the second occasion against it, because they saw it would be adverse to their party interests. But this state of things would not last for ever. (Laughter.) It would not always be the case that the minority in the town would command a majority in the Council. It would be rectified one of ' these days. and he would advise the Conservatives not to allow the reproach to be thrown upon them that they had abused their power. (Applause, and cries of " Vote.") The voting was then proceeded with, and the papers having been filled up and handed to the Mayor they were read out as follows For Comic:Dor John Crosfield—Alderman J Davies, Alderman J Burgess, Alderman C J Holmes; Councillors J H Fleming, J Platt, W Pierpoint, H Roberts, F Dixon, J Brown, G Dakin, J Barker, T J Ridgway, J Greening, E Milner, C Broadbent. For Councillor Thomas Sutton—Alderman S M Webster, Councillors Dr Mackie, T lintchineon, J Taylor, J Pier- point, J Ashton, It W Marsh, W Tinsley, W Beam:, R W Francomb, J E Wright, W J Burgess, T Litton. The Mason said he was glad to be relieved of voting at all, but added that if he had, been called upon to vote he would have given his support to Councillor Sutton. He stated that the numbers were as follows:— For Councillor Crosfield For Councillor Sutton He therefore declared Councillor Crosfield drily elected an alderman of the borough. (Applause.) Alderman Devues here stated that had Alderman Pick. mere been able to be present that night he would have voted for Councillor Crosfield. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BuaGass said he wished to endorse what Alderman Davies had just said, that the election would not alter the numbers of the polical parties in thet Council, as there would be no attempt by the Liberal party to wrest the vacant seat from the Conservatives. Councillor PLATT said he would not accept that state- ment, and,he didn't know who warranted Alderman Burgess in saying it. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Alderman CROSFIELD,who was received with applause, said: I need not tell you that I have sat here to-night in great pain. It has been a most disagreeable hour to me. In the first place, I may tell you candidly that I had no desire whatever to hold this office, and it makes me very encona- fortable because I feel that there is a gentlemen in this Council who ought to have been elected to the office before me—l refer to my friend Councillor Broadbent. (Hear, hear) I am very sorry that my name should have caused such an exhibition of feeling or temper in this Council Chamber. We generally avoid personalities here, and they are better kept in the back ground. (Hear, hear.) Coun- cillor Dr. Mackie has referred to me as having done some- thing to him. I have no remembrance whatever of it, and if I did as he said I must have done so officially, and not from any personal feeling. (Councillor Dr. Mackie : "True.") I must also be allowed to remark that this Coun- cil Chamber for the last 10 or 15 years has certainly not improved. I fear it has degenerated. You cannot ety that the leading gentlemen in Warrington are members of the Council, and if you ask what is the reason, I fear it is be- cause these matters are conducted upon merely political motives. (Hear, hear.) I should like to see gentlemen in this Council Chamber who are the large manufacturers, but I don't think you will get them to come here if this kind of thing is to be done—this acting entirely from political motives. There is something higher than politics, and that is patriotism. (Applause.) The first consideration of every gentleman in this room, and every one out of it, ought to be to do that which is best for the town irrespective of politics. (Hear, bear.) The good ef a town I say is before party prosperity, and I for one, as a member of the Liberal party, will never consent to give my vote for a Liberal in this chamber as against a Conservative unless I consider he is the best man. (Hear, hear.) I say that it would have been a disgrace to this Council if Aldermen Burgess and Holmes had not been elected aldermen when they were. I am very thankful that we did retain their services, because from the length of time they have been here they are fully entitled to have such a confidence placed in them. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, I beg to thank you for the vote you have given me, and I must say again that I am very sorry indeed that the position ef alderman has not fallen to the lot of someone more worthy of it than I am. (Applause.) Councillor BROADBENT said it would be folly to pretend to ignore the fact of party feeling in this town, and in all other towns, but he was sorry to hear anyone get up and say "This is not a question of persons at all ' • it is mere ic polits. I will vote for any man, good or bad, if he belongs to my party, and if be does not I will vote against him," He was sorry that that sort of spirit should get into the Council, and he thought they ought to do their best to elect those men who had served the town best. (Hear, hear.) Councillor SUTTON thanked the members of the Council who had supported him, and stated that personally he had not sought the honour of election. He was brought for- ward by the party with which he was connected, and, of 'course, he did not consider it was his duty to refuse to be nominated. They could not overlook the fact that that had been a party election with this simple difference. The Liberal party, the party with which Mr. Crosfield was con- nected, had been, as they always were whenever a party elec•ion took place in the Council Chamber, true to a man to themselves; while on the other hand the party with which be happened to be connected, soma of them at all events, for reasons of their own, either absented themselves
from the meetings of the Council en OCCAMOMS like these or voted against their party. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. Meadowcroft said he did not think that a statement of th it kind should have so irritated the law clerk as to induce him to eater into a defence of his action in the matter to a person outside the Board. After some further conversation on this point, the pro- ceedings terminated. WIDNES OPPOSITION.

Yesterday afternoon, the Widnes Local Board held a special meeting for the purpose of adopting a petition to the House of Lords against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. Mr F H Clossage presided,. and there were also present, Messrs o•Keeffe, Sadler, Martley, Houghton, Midwood. Wright, Forster, klandley, Allen (clerk), an Robert Davies, ' of Warrington (solicitor to the Board.) During the course of the proceedings, the chairman said he had obtained some figures as to the dock and canal traffic, which might be of interest to the Board. The vessels passing in and out of Widnes dock and St Helens canal in the year 1884 were as follow :—Widnes dock about 483 per month, and the canal about 1,050 per month, making a total of 18,304 for the year. The number of vessels passing in and out of West Bank dock for the year was 3.884, making a total of 22,278 for the two dock& during the 12 months. After some explanations as to the local course to be pursued, given by Mr Davies, a petition t.) the House of Lords was unani- mously adopted against the Bill, on the motion of Mr Handley, seconded by Mr Wright. OPPOSITION FROM ST. HELENS.

A special meeting of the St. Helens Town Council was heid at the Town Hall on Wednesday afternoon to consider the expediency of opposing the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, now pending in Parliament, and to sanction the cost of such opposition if determined upon out of the borough rates. COuncillor R. Pilkingtou proposed that the town clerk be instructed to take all necessary steps for the due Drotaction of the rights and interests of the borough of St. Helens, more especially with regard to the Sankey Canal and the entrances therefrom into the Mersev.—Councillor H. Baxter seconded the proposal, which, on being put, was carried by 15 votes to 5. MEETING OF PROVISIONAL COMMITTEE.

The weekly meeting of the Provisional Commit'es was held in the Board-room, 70e, Market-street, Manchester, on Friday afternoons Mr. Henry Boddington, jun., presiding, in the absence of the chairman of the cemmittee, who was in London endeavouring to facilitate the progress of the Bill. It was announced that there was no possibility of a joint committee, but that proceedings before the first Select Com- mittee—House of Lords—would tie commenced at the earliest possible date, very probably on Thursday next. With this in view all the arrangements for the opening of the case by Mr. Pembsr, Q.O , on that day and the ample- tion of the evidence are being accelerated. The proceed- ings of the Parliamentary Sub-committee, whicn included a report of a further inspection of the estuary by the en- gineers retained for the Bill were submitted, from which it appeared that a large number of minor matters had been disposed of as affecting the interests of various landowners and others. Considerable support continues to be accorded in the shape of subscriptions to the Parliamentary expenses, and the Provisional Committee anticipate still further in- crease in this direction.

The Wesleyans have decided to start a mission in the worst rookeries of London, and to raise a fund of .£25,000. The Queen has commissioned Mr J E Boehm to execute a marble bast of the late General Gordon for the gallery at Windsor Castle.
At a fire which occurred on Sunday midnight at a tailor- ing establishment in Glaegow, two women who lived in the shop were burned to death.

dontinned complaints of the state of the cotton trade come from all parts of North and East Lancashire, and other mills are being put en short time. It is expected that the Supplementary Estimate for the expenses already incurred in connection with the war in the Soudan will amonnt to about £1,500,000. The evidence on behalf of the Countess of Durham in the suit instituted by her husband for a declaration of nullity of marriage was concluded on Thursday. On Friday, Lord Durham's nullity suit was resumed. The Attorney-General then addressed the court for the respondent, and the Solici- tor-General then replied. INDEPENDENT METHODISTIL—For Some years past the Independent Methodists of the Warrington Circuit have been making efforts to establish a branch of the society in Earlestown ; and success would appear to have recently at- tended their efforts. As a commencement, special services were held on Sunday in a building, No. 19, Back Market- street, which bad been temporarily fitted up for the pur- pose. In the afternoon the service was conducted by Mr W Hudson, of Warrington, and in the evening by Mr W Mercer, of Lymm. On each occasion there was a crowded attendance. For the present, it is proposed to continuo the services each Sunday in the same pl?.ce. SUBSTITUTE FOR BUTTER, a 2lbs Jar Real Raspberry and Gooseberry Jam, sid. TEST NEWS.

Prince Henry of Battenburg arrived at Charing Cross terminus on Friday morning, from Germany. Cmnt Munster, the German Ambassador, had an inter- view with Earl Granville at the hatter's private residence, on Friday morning. Mr. F. W. Alicock, of the firm of Alicock Brothers, general brassfounders, of Birmingham, has committed suicide in a Manchester hotel. It has been unofficially intimated to the local authorities that the Prince and Princess of Wales will arrive at Lon- donderry by the Northern Counties Railway about the 10th pros. The work of making a safe passage through the great fall in the Maudlin seam of the Unsworth Colliery has not yet been completed, but it is hoped the explorers will be able to reenme operations in a few hours. THE SHOW:WRYNESS EXPLOSION' : ANOTHER Dirent.—Tbe Inquest on these killed by the recent shell explosion at Shoeburynesewas concluded on Friday. The chief witness was Mr Robert Lowe, assistant manager of the Royal Labo- ratory, Woolwich Arsenal, who was seriously injured in the explosion, and whose evidence was taken by the jury at the Rospital where be lay in bed. Mr. Lowe minutely described the nature of the experiment. The fuse which caused the explosion was a newly invented one, and was considered ab- solutely safe. Other witnesses having been examined, the jury returned a verdict of accidental death 4 dding that they did not consider anybody was to blame. Mr. Rance, of Woolwich Arsenal, died of his wounds on Friday after- neoon, and a formal inquiry, which was at once held on the body, resulted also in a verdict of accidenta:. death.

div.head: ELECTION OF Arrilroas.
div.p: ELECTION OF Arrilroas.
Tbe TOWN CLERK announced that Messrs John Hari son and J L Tunstall had been elected elective auditors, and Mr Councillor Brown as Mayor's auditor.
THE PAVING OF BEIDGE-STEBE'T;

The Itfavou said be had received a memorial which had been signed by a considerable number of influential inhabi- tants in Bridge-street. It was as follows :—" To the Town Council,—We. the undersigned, being occupiers of property in Bridge-street, having beard the proposal of the Paving and Sewerage Committee to pave that part of Bridge-street between Priars'-gate and Bylands-street with setts, bag re- spectfully to urge upon the Corporation to pave Bridge- street with wood instead of stone. We may point out that our property is highly rented, and consequently highly rated, and that as we paw very largely towards the rates of the town,. we ask for some extended consideration as to the , way in which the street should be paved,, so as to interfere as little as possible with the use and enjoyment of our pro- perty. We btlieve that if the street is paved with stone setts it will be very prejudicial to us, and we therefore re- soectfully beg the Council to pave the street with wood."— The memorial was referred to the Paving Committee.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING.

Councillor BURGESS moved that the motion which stood in his name with regard to Sunday closing be taken before the proceedings of the cmimittees —Councillor Dixox seconded the proposal, which, on being put to the meeting was, however, not carried.

div.head: COMMITTEES.
div.p: THE COMMITTEES.
TEle minutes of the Watch, Financ.e, and Street Im• provement and Lighting Committee were confirmed without discussion.
THE MEASLES, &C.

The sanitary Cenunittees' minates contained a recom- mendation that an order be made under section 23 of the Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act, 1879, declaring that section to apply to measles and whoop- ing cough, for a period of three years, and that the town clerk be instructed to apply to the Local Government Board for their qanction r, such an order. _

Alderman BURGESS moved the confirmation, and Coun- cillor BARKER seconded. Councillor W. PIERPGINT moved, and Councillor Bun- GESS seconded an amendment that no application be made to the Local Government Board as above indicated. They objected to diseases like measles and whooping cough being put into the same category as the more dangerous infec- tious diseases. On the amendment being put 11 voted in its favour and 12 against, and it was consequently not carried.

THE PROPOSED EXTENSIONS AT LONGFORD. The Sanitary Committee's minutes containedthe follow- in % recommendations :—Recommendationa that a plot of freehold land off Birchall-street, containing about 3,800 square yards, be purchased from Mr. William Sharp, at 4s 71 per yard, for the purposes of an intercepting depot, in connection with the proposed extensions at Longford, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board. Recommendation, that a plot of land, containing about 1,800 square yards, en the south side of the works belonging to Messrs Rcberts, Dale, and Co, Mersey-street, be leased from Messrs Roberts, Dale, and Co, at 4d per yard, for the purposes of an intercepting depot, in connection with the proposed extensions at Longford, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board.

Some discussion took place on these recommendations, in the midst of which it was moved that the Council adjourn till Tuesday next, and a petition against the bills respecting railway rates and charges having teen agresd to unani. money, the motion for adjournment was carried.

MEE PING OF SHIPOWNERS. On Thursday morning; a meeting of the shipowners of Thlinorn Tfa4 held ai the office of Mr R B Toft, Bottom 'Locke, to consider the Bill. Mr R B Toft presided. As the Board of Commissioners have been empowered to oppose .the Bill in the Interests of the toe n, the meetLV: considered it unnecessary that the shipowners should take separate action, and the following resolution was passed That this meeting approves in general of the clauses submitted by the Runcorn Commissioners for the protection of the trade and port of Runcorn, and is willing to render what- eYer support may be deemed necessary." A deputation consisting of Messrs It B Toft, Richard Clarke, and W J Shore was appointed to confer with the Commissioners if desired.

div.head: MEETING OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: MEETING OF COMMISSIONERS.

On Thursday evening a special meeting of the Board of Commissioners was held at the Town Hall to affix the seal of the Board to a petition in ParHimont against the MALI. cheater Ship Canal 8,11. Mr R Shaw presided, and there were other 14 members present.—ln opening the meeting, the Chairman made a speech of considerable length in vin- dication of the conduct of the Commissioners. Referring to the technical objection made by Dr McDougall as te the posting of the notices respecting the ratepayers' meeting, he showed that tbe law had been complied with, and contended that if the meeting had been permitted to discuss fairly the real question at issue, the ratepayers would then have given their adhesion, as they had done since, to the requirements which the Commissioners considered were necessary for the protection of the port of Runcorn. He combated the state- ment that the Board ought to have taken steps earlier, and pointed out that there was no middle course—either the Board must or must not oppose the Bill. Under the Bill as it at present was, it would be impossible to carry on the trade of the docks, and he thought the Board would have been neglecting their duty had not they strained ever' nerve to put before the ratepayers what they believed to be for their benefit, and for the benefit of future generations, and the ratepayers had now expressed the opinion that the Board was right. Notwithstanding all the attempts made to dis- parage the gentlemen of the Board, he hoped the members would continue to do what they believed would be for the benefit and prosperity of the town. (hear, hear, and ap- plauee).—The LAW Clerk said towards the 14th or 15th January he was charged upon what was said to be a state. ment made by the chairman of the Board with neglecting the interests of the ratepayers in not submitting clauses which he bed been instructed to prepare on the 24th Dec. The Law Clerk replied that he had not been called in until the 24th December, although the communication from the promoters of the Ship Canal bad been received by the Com- miesioners early in October.—The Chairman said the com- mittee got together a large amount of information written in black and white, and then asked the Law Clerk to put it in legal form. After that there ought not to have been much delay in preparing clauses —The Law Clerk stated, and he was confirmed by Mr. Pritchard, that several of the clauses had to be remodelled about the middle of January. He added that it was very unpleasant that an officer should be charged by a member of the Board in this way. He then read the petition which had been prepared, setting forth the injurious effect the scheme would have upon the Interests of the port if curbed out as proposed.— Mr. Pritchard moved that the seal of the Board be affixed to the petition. He narrated the proceedings of the commit- tee since October, quoted correspondence that bad passed be- tween the Board and 'the promoters, and said no blame could possibly be attached to the Commissioners. They had from the first pushed forward the matter, and made every attempt possible to settle the clauses in a satisfactory man- ner. Alluding to the ratepayers' meeting, held en the sth tilt., Mr. Pritchard said the object of the opposition was evidently to disperse the meeting by raising a technical objection altogether irrelevant to the point at issue. The poll on the previous Monday, he held, was a sufficient vindication of the conduct of the Commissioners, and an emphatic condemnation of the leaders of the opposition on the sth February. (hear, hear.) The traders and ship- owners were at one with the Board in trying to obtain the clauses, and said they looked to the Commissioners to pro- tect and' secure their interests. The action of the leaders of the opposition on the sth February had had the following effects: 1. It weakened the hands of the Commissioners and made it hopeless at that time to negotiate with any pros- pect of success; 2, It has caused a delay of one month as on the 6th February they would have been in communication with the promoters, endeavouring to arrange their clauses; 3, They had put the town to the expense of a poll, which would cost some £5O or £6O; 4, It had necessitated the peti- tion to Parliament, with probably the farther expense of sending a deputation to London to follow the promoters. Mr Lightburn seconded the motion. He thought by the poll the Commissioners had a strong vote of confidence passed in them, for if they analysed the figures they found that, apart from the plurality of votes of property owners, there were 1,128 votes in favour of the opposition, and 361 against. That calculation was made on the basis of t, one man, one vote." The Commissioners in this case had been shown to he incontestably right. When they were shown to be wrong there was not a priltest. He asked where WAS the consistency of those from whom we have the misfortune to differ now?

The motion was unanimously Carried. The Chairman, on signing the petition, said he bad the pleasure of signing a similar petition before that day, and other people besides the Commissioners were of opinion that they had taken the proper course in the matter. Tbe Ltw Clerk said Dr. MacDougall came to his °Mee ene day and told him that it had been stated that the whole of the delay in connection with the preparation of the clauses rested upon his (Mr. Linaker'e) shoulders, lie informed Dr. MacDougall that the first communication of the promo- ters to the Commissioners came in October' and that he (the law clerk) had not been called on until the 24th Decem- ber. Beyond that Dr. MacDougall had received no in- formation from him. He (Mr. Linaker) had had no come munio Ition at all in writing, and could, therefore, give none. He bad been applied to by many people for documents, but be had declined to supply them. He had made that ex- planation because it was well known that Dr. MacDougall iwas a personal friend of his own.

div.head: ATTEMPTED ASSAS3INATION OF A JUDGE.
div.p: ATTEMPTED ASSAS3INATION OF A JUDGE.

REFINE, FRIDAY EVENING.—During the hearing of a lib4l case at Lausanne to-day, a witness made a desperate attempt to kill the judge with a revolver. He wounded three officials before he could be secured. ENGLAND AND BUSSIA.

The Centr,l News learns that after the Russian A.mbas- I sador had left Mr. Gladstone on Thursday afternoon, im- portant despatches were received from St. Petersburg, which were couched in language of the same re-assuring character as that addressed personally by M. De Steal to the Premier early in the day ; but it is stated that despite the friendly tenour of the despatches there is no indication of any in- tention on the part of the Russian Government to withdraw their advanced posts from the disputed Afghan territory. On the:contrary, it is plausibly argued that Afghanistan can have no claim to the ground now occupied by Russia, who is prepared to offer the most distinct pledges that no further advance will be made by her towards Herat. Thus the latest Russian note does little more than offer another "Re-assu- rance " to the British Government. In the meantime, Sir Peter Lumsden strongly urges that the Russian advanced posts shall be withdrawn irons such close proximity to the Afghan forces previous to the commencement of the actual work of delimitating the frontier. In this matter the repre- sentations ef the British Commissioner are receiving the energetic support of the highest personages in the realm, and there is every reason to believe that our Government will again press for the evacuation of the disputed territory by the Russian Vedettes. The British Government await with anxiety farther despatches from Sir Peter Lurnsden, the intention of Ministers being more deeply centred in his reports than in the explanations of Russia in this coun- try. AX.—gati üBL VILLE made a statement in referenCe to Prince Birmarck'S recent remarks in the German Reichstag, as to his making public certain communications regarded +as confidential respecting Egypt. His lordship explained LILO he wethl reply to the personal charges in another way. Pidet.e bis- marck had misunderstood certain remarks that he had trA,Me in reply to the Duke of Richmond as being applied to himself. He regretted there should have'been any misunderstanding. Hs said there was no country in the world in which not only politicians but people of all classes more fully ap- preciated the very great and important position which Germany held than this country. He felt that in the in- terests of Europe the relations between England and Ger- many should be of the most friendly character. No efforts would ba wanting on his part to carry out the conciliatory declaration of policy sketched out the other day by the German Chancellor.

THE NAVY.—Lord Noirrninzoos, replying to Viscount Sidmentla, stated that there bad been no delay in carrying out the additions to the Navy announced last autumn. Government had intended to build thirty new torpedo boats, of which ten had been ordered. In reply to the Earl of Clanwilliam' he said the forty-three ton guns which had been ordered had proved entirely satisfactory, and would be supplied to vessale ordered for them next year. The House shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. QUESTIONS.—A new writ was issued for Glasgow in room of Mr. G. Anderson, resigned.—Mr, CoWEN gave notice that on that day three weeks he should draw attention to the pro- ceedings of Germany in the Cameroons, and move a resolu- tion.—Lonn HARTINGTON replying to Mr. Chaplin said he could give no information of the intentions ot the Govern- ment of India on the subject of the Afghanistan frontier.— Sir. T. BRASSEY replying to Mr. Gourley, said the repairs of the Victoria and Albert yacht would be completed in a fort- night. The cost was £sB,ooo.—Mr. theereeroxie replying to Sir Stafford Northcote said the Vote of Credit would not be asked for before the Budget was brought forward, neither of which he thought would take place before Easter. THE SEATS BILL —On the motion to go into Com- mittee on the Redistribution Bill, Mr PARNELL called atten- tion to the jerrymandering of the Irish Boundary Commis- sioners in the province of Ulster, and accused them of taking representatives from Roman Catholics wherever they had opportunity, in compliance with directions from Lord Spencer.—Mr SHAW LEFEVRE defended the Irish Boundary Commemioners, and gave direct denial to the statement that they had acted in accordance with directions from Earl Spencer. He was prepared to prove in every case the Commissioners had acted rightly, and in accord- ance with instructions given them.—Mr PetneKerr cen- sured the course pursued by the member for Cork.—Mr BRIMMED thought the loyalists in Ireland had cause to cemplain.—The Lome; ADVOCATE informed the member for Kilmarnock that some alteration had been made in the pro- posals regarding Scotch boroughs, and the Government were prepared to give due consideration to any fnrther sug- gestions that might be made on the subject.—The motion. that the Speaker leave the chair was agreed to after further discussion. The House then went into eommittee on the bill —Mr. BRYCE then moved an amendment to clause I with the view of including the universities in the schedule.—Sir C. DIME intimated that the clause being the result of I arrangement between the tw3 great parties, it was im- possible for them to accept the amendment.—Sir Stafford Northcote and Mr. Gladstone opposed the amendment.— After a long discussion a motion to report progress was agreed to. The House adjourned at 5-minutes to 1.

TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH-WEST WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEDINN,—At the urgent request of a large number of Ratepayers I have consented to allow myself to be nominated for the vacancy in the representation of this Ward in the Town C runcil, caused by the election of Councillor John Orcsfield as an Alderman of the Borough. As a native of Warrington, the good government of the Borough at large, is to me a matter of great importance, and having resided for many years in the south-West Ward, it la only natural that. if elected, I shou'd be especially desirous of promoting the interests of my neighbours and fellow rate- payers, I think that the present depressed condition of trade calla for the practice r f the strictest porsible economy consistent with prudence and efficiency in every department of municipal work, and if you honour me with your confidence, I shall spare no effort to aid in such an administration of our Town's Affairs as will help to frustrate any unnecessary expenditure and will promote a permanent reduction of the rates. Respectfully requesting your support, I beg to remain, ladies and gentlemen, Your obedient servant, CHARLES SAWKINS BURGESS. 31, Bold-etreet, Warrington, March sth. 1885.
APOLOGY. IBeg to withdraw the words I used against the Irish Naticonal League, and to apologise for hav:ng made use of thorn, Signed, JOHN 11, Napier,street, Warrington.

RUNCORN IMPktUVEMbNT CO VIMItaSIONERS.— MANCHESTAR SHIP CANAL.—At a duly convened meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, held in the Town Hall, Waterloo-road. Runcorn, on Thursday, the sth day of February, it was unanimously resolved—" That the Runeern Improvement, 0-anmissioners oppose, in Parliament, a private Bill, Intituled • A Bill to authorize the construction of a Ship Canal to Manchester, and for other purposes,' and that the Parliamentary and Legal Committee, with Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, be and are hereby empowereel and Instructed to take all necetsary steps by petition to Parliament, and other- wise,for giving effect to such opposition, and for the protection of the rights and interests of the Board and of the district of Runcorn, in relation to the objects of such Bill. That the costs and expenees. whether already incurred or to be incurred, of and attendant upon the Commissioners' opposition to the said Bill, be eharged upon the general district; rate, or other the public funds or rates under the control of the said Commis- sioners. W. BROOKES, Secretary. Town Hall, Runcorn, March sth, 1555.

IN PARLIAMENT.—Busion 1883. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. VV. HEREAS a MEETING of the OWNERS and RATEPAYE 413 of the Improvement Act District of Runcorn. in the 0 unty of Cheshire, was held on Thursday, the sth day of February, 1885, in tba Bethesda School-room, Vicar-street, Runcorn, in pursuance of the Act of the 35th and 36th Vic., cap. 91, intituled "An Act to authorize the ap- plication of Funds of Municipal Corporations and other govern- lag bodies in certain oases ;” And Whereas at the. said Meeting, held at the time and place aforesaid, I, as Chairman of such meeting, and in com- pliance with the statute, prorosed the following resolution : That the consent of the Owners and Ratepayers of the Im- provement Act Distr ct of Runcorn be. and the same is hereby, gtva to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners to'-Oppose in Parliament a Private Bill now before Parliament, intituied, ' A. Bill to authorize the construction of a Ship Canal to Man- Chester, and for other purposes,' and this meeting hereby ap- proves and santions the applying of the General District Rate, or other the Public Funds or Rates under the control of the said Improvement Commissioners, to the payment of the costs and expenses attending such oppze'tion ;" And Whereas the said resolution on being put to the meet- ing Was not carried, whereupon demand was made that such question should be decided by a Poll of the Owners and Rate- payers; And Whereas a Poll was accordingly taken in manner pro. vided by the Public Health Act, 180, and the PChedules thereto. I hereby declare that at such Poll of the Owners and Rate- payers, the above resolution was carr'ed. Dated at Runcorn this 2nd day of March, 1885. ROBERT SHAW, Returning Ofileer.
